A sunny Mexican market stall run by one beaming chef, where the whole game is a grill: three chilis in traffic-light colours sit on three plates above the reels, catch fire to start the Hold & Win, and turn the day street into a lantern-lit fiesta night.

Art direction Read

StyleFamily animated-feature illustration throughout: a storybook street, a soft caricature chef, plump glossy food symbols and comic poster lettering. Unlike many games of this kind there is no gap between a realistic world and stylised game pieces; background, character and symbols share one rounded, friendly manner, the symbols only more saturated and glossier. Inference: the two street pictures and the chef have the look of an image model's work finished by hand (the night street repeats the day street object for object); frame, boards, lettering and effects are drawn in the usual production way.
RenderingBackgrounds: painted gradients with brush texture and no outlines. Chef: smooth 3D-like shading with a warm rim. Symbols: strong gradients, long white speculars, a dark outline, each on the dark plank board. Lettering: two-tone gradients with a top bevel, dark outline and lower extrusion. Fire: cel-painted licks in two or three tones with a soft glow. Smoke and light: white sprites tinted by the engine.
ColourMeasured over the game's art: dusty wine #60373f 12%, dark wine #371819 12%, terracotta #b45832 11%, sand #ca996b 10%, near-white #f5f7f5 9%, mauve #7e5966 8%, pale sand #eac596 8%, gold #fbd945 2%. A warm palette of cream, terracotta and red with green as the foil. Colour carries the rules: green, yellow and red for the three chilis, in value order (1x, 2x, 5x the stake), repeated on their words, their effect marks and the logo; red and gold, orange, cyan and purple for GRAND, MAJOR, MINOR and MINI; cyan, orange and red for BIG, SUPER and MEGA WIN; one hue per letter symbol. The bonus keeps every game piece and changes the world to violet and deep blue with orange lights.
LightingBase game: high sun from the upper right, soft short shadows. Bonus: moonlight with warm pools from windows, a lantern and strings of bulbs. Game pieces carry their own top light and do not take the scene's; fire lights itself and gives the chilis a rim.
AmbienceA holiday lunch at a street grill: sunny, generous, a little comic (the deadpan hen, the chef who breathes fire and coins when the chilis ignite). The bonus is the same street at fiesta time, hotter and more intimate.
ShapesRound and plump everywhere: curved chilis, barrel cacti, a domed sombrero, a round-faced chef, rounded slab letters. The chili silhouette is the game's mark and is reused as a shape: the logo sign and win plate are a chili-shaped wooden board, a glow has a chili-shaped hole, the coin is embossed with a chili. Zigzag bands (poncho, sombrero, letters) are the second repeated motif.
MaterialsStucco, terracotta and clay tile; bleached and red-painted wood, rope; steel grill plates, cold and red-hot; waxy pepper skin, straw, feathers, glass; flame, smoke, gold coin.
TypographyDrawn words in rounded comic capitals with a double outline for the logo, the jackpots, the win tiers, the chili words (SPICY, HOT, BURNS) and the headings BONUS GAME, JACKPOT, TOTAL WIN and CONGRATS!, each in its rule colour. Rules on the bonus splash are a condensed italic sans in white with a red edge. Numbers come from three bitmap fonts of the provider's shared store: Tsiyugunsini in gold with a wine-red edge (jackpot values, the value on every Chili symbol, win amounts), Ultra in black with a gold rim (the +1 and x2 effect marks), Contrail One in white (the jackpot counters); which font sets which number is an inference from comparing glyphs with the screens. The shell's Poppins sets the help, buttons and balance line.
MotionAll character and layout motion is Spine: 37 skeletons in one bundle file (35 in 4.2.43, one in 4.1.24, one in 4.3.26), with 12 frame sequences (204 frames) that are almost all fire and smoke: a 31-frame fire burst, an 18-frame flame behind each Chili symbol, flame splashes, fire lines and streaks, a 28-frame cloud, puffs, an 18-frame smoke wisp, sparkles and a 10-frame coin. Seen in play: flames behind the three chilis on the intro; win lines as a thin gold line; a win amount on the wooden pepper plate with coins; the grill chilis lifting and flaring as their symbols land; on the bonus trigger all three ignite, the chef claps his hands to his mouth and blows fire and coins, the words turn into +1, x2 and an up-arrow; the Bonus Game splash on a tall red board; a red-orange fire screen with the grill and the three chilis as the change of scene; a golden flash with the chef giving two thumbs up as the game opens; then, in the bonus, the night street, a row of red chilis added on top inside a gold outline, values growing as +1 and x2 marks fly down, and empty positions burning as a reel nears full. When a reel fills, its chilis fly up to the wooden pepper plate, which counts the win; the MINI jackpot came with the gold JACKPOT word, the tier word large over the reels, coins and streamers; TOTAL WIN closes the bonus on the tall red board. Read from the files only: BIG, SUPER and MEGA WIN and the three higher jackpots. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer cannot draw Spine 4; assembled and motion pictures are absent for that reason only.
VariantsTwo scenes on one composition (day and night). Three chilis on one rig with three skins, in symbol, grill and splash sizes. Three collectors on one rig with three skins. Four jackpot boards on one plank. Three win tiers on one lettering. Two reel backings (three rows, and four with the bonus row) and a frame cut in mirrored strips so the board can grow. One chef with three pairs of hands. One wooden pepper board used as logo sign, bonus counter panel and win plate.
ConstructionTwo 4096 px atlas pages hold the whole game: each carries one 2750x2582 scene, and the rest is some 340 small sprites, more than half of them fire and smoke frames. Twelve word pictures are localised files (en-GB loaded). The chef is a bust of 19 parts with one painted face; the Wild hen is 12 parts; every other symbol is one to three sprites on a shared rig with skins. Effects are reused across skeletons by name (the symbol flame is also the grill flame, tinted red for a second version; the Wild's smoke is also the grill's). White effect sprites are tinted in the engine. The symbol pictures for the help, the flat logo, the numeral fonts, the Buy Feature cards, the controls and Poppins come from the provider's shared store outside the game bundle. The artists' white cell guide (tileGuide) and green container guide ship in the atlas as anchors.
ConsistencyHigh. One manner runs from street to chef to symbols, and the three chili colours tie logo, symbols, grill, words, effect marks and poncho stripes together. The seams are small: the black-and-gold slab numerals of the effect marks and the condensed italic rule text are stock type beside hand-drawn comic capitals, and the Buy Feature cards are denser and hotter than anything in play.

What to take from it Read

  • Turn the mechanic into a place in the scene. The three persistent bonus modifiers are three chilis on a grill above the reels, each with a plate that heats, a word and a dial; the player reads the state of the game from a picture of cooking, not from meters.
  • Use an order people already know for value. Green, yellow, red is 1x, 2x, 5x and nobody needs it explained; the same three colours then pay for the logo, the words, the effect marks and the costume.
  • One host character, cut cheaply, gives a game a face. The chef is a bust with one painted face, separate brows, eyelids and moustache, and three pairs of forearms; his big moment (hands to mouth, fire and coins) is hand swaps and particles, not a new drawing.
  • Keep background, character and symbols in one style when the theme is warm and comic. Here nothing is photoreal, so no dark board trick is needed to separate symbols from the world: saturation and gloss do it.
  • Make the bonus by changing the time of day. The night street is the same composition relit, with every game piece unchanged; it reads as a new place for the cost of one picture.
  • Spend the frame budget where the theme lives. More than half of the sprites are fire and smoke frames, painted in a cel style that matches the illustration, and each loop is reused by several rigs and tinted for variants.
  • Reuse one themed silhouette as a container. The chili-shaped wooden board is the logo sign, the bonus panel and the win plate; the same shape is cut into a glow and embossed on the coin.
  • Draw the short words, set the numbers. SPICY, HOT, BURNS, the jackpots and win tiers are drawn pictures in the rule colour; every amount is a bitmap font, so one pepper carries any value and the +1 and x2 marks can fly as text.
  • Plan localisation of drawn text early: twelve word pictures ship per language here, while the chili words are English inside the art and are not localised.
  • For AI-assisted art: the two street scenes and a host bust are where an image model gives most (a relit copy of one composition is exactly its strength); the symbols must then be pushed to the same manner at higher gloss, and the grill states, the frame in strips, the lettering and the effect loops are production work to plan as parts and frames from the start.

A classic fruit-and-sevens machine staged as a neon cabinet flying through giant 3D 777 signs: the whole game is three colours of one flaming seven, each tied to a jackpot of its colour, on a backdrop that flips from purple night to orange blaze.

Art direction Read

StyleGlossy sticker-like symbols with gold keylines, Western slab-serif lettering, and neon line work, on an abstract backdrop of light rays. The only solid scenery is a set of pre-rendered 777 blocks in steep perspective. Nothing is a character and nothing is a place.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed enamel with one hard glint on symbols; flat neon outlines with glow for plaques, frames and jackpot wins; flat two-tone cartoon fire and white lightning for effects; soft gradient rays for the ground. Every symbol carries its own keyline and halo.
ColourMeasured over the game's art: near-black purple #1f0a2c 27%, red #9d2117 14%, orange #e96d0f 13%, gold #f9c013 11%, light golds #fdfbf3 and #fbed86 9% together, hot red #f11f07 3%, dark blue #0c0872 1%. The code is three hues: blue for the single seven and MINI, purple for the double seven and MINOR, red for the triple seven and MAJOR, repeated on symbol, plaque, jackpot win, gem and particle. Gold is the Wild, the frame, the logo and every amount. Cyan appears only as electricity.
LightingAlmost everything is self-lit: neon, lamps behind plates, fire. Symbols have a conventional upper-left light and a warm halo. The backdrop's light comes from one vanishing point behind the cabinet.
AmbienceA machine in a dark club, humming with neon, that catches fire when a feature starts. The base game is cool and purple, Free Spins and the intro are orange and red; the cabinet itself does not change.
ShapesThe seven above all: as symbol, jackpot plaque silhouette, win plate, 3D block and logo. Around it a pinched cabinet outline, chevrons, diamonds on the win lines, thin dotted bulb lines, fat slab letters.
MaterialsEnamel, polished gold, neon tube, back-lit glass, fruit skin, cut gems, fire, electric arc.
TypographyOne voice: fat Western slab serifs. Drawn words for the logo, WILD, FREE SPINS, the jackpot names and the win tiers (gold to orange with a dark blue shadow); three bitmap numeral fonts from the provider's shared font store (UltraGold large, UltraActive and UltraInactive small). The help, the buttons and the balance line are the shell's Poppins.
MotionAll motion is Spine: 46 skeletons in two bundle files (44 in 4.2.43, two particle layers in 4.1.24), most of them scene layers and effects moving still pictures, with 22 hand-drawn frame sequences (398 frames: outline traces, fire, lightning, tumbling gems, a turning coin, the logo burning). Seen in play: the logo breaking up among coins after START, neon frames breathing, 777 blocks drifting behind the cabinet, cyan arcs on the frame and bolts at the jackpots, a gold seven flying from a Wild to the plaques, a lightning column on the last reel before a trigger, three sevens turning red on the splash, fire across the screen into Free Spins, Wilds locking, a BIG WIN and a MINOR jackpot win with gold rays and coins. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7; assembled and motion pictures are absent for that reason only.
VariantsTwo backdrop states (Normal, Special) for the ground and for each of eight 777 block views; one seven in four colourings (blue, purple, red, gold) and three counts; three jackpot plaques and three jackpot win plates from one idea; three win tiers and a total from one layout; lit and unlit paytable plates and numerals.
ConstructionThree 4096 px atlas pages hold 518 sprites, with two of the pages roughly half empty; the ground is a mirrored half; words are separate from what they label, and six lettering files are localised (en-GB). The paytable pictures, the help logo, the buy card, the numeral fonts, the Double Chance card, the controls and Poppins come from the provider's shared services. Compared with Fire Rail Express (run 2026-11-26-1556) from the files: the shell, Poppins and the Double Chance card are the same; 40 sprites are pixel for pixel the same (36 white flame frames, the white starburst, a glow, a glow square, a white box); 23 of the 46 skeleton names are the same (Backgrounds, Logo, SlotFrame, Jackpot, WinBig, WinTotal, TileWild and others), which points to one scene template; the pictures under shared names such as bgNormal, bgSpecial and jackpotFrame are different. Everything that carries the theme is this game's own.
ConsistencyVery high, by economy: one seven, one letter style, three hues and gold. The one piece outside the system is the painted buy card, and it shows the same cast.

What to take from it Read

  • One drawing can be a whole high-symbol set: a single flaming seven, recoloured three times and repeated one, two or three times, gives the ranks, and the same seven in gold is the Wild and the logo.
  • Tie each top symbol to a prize by colour and by shape: blue 7 to the blue one-seven MINI plaque, purple 77 to MINOR, red 777 to MAJOR. The rule is readable without a word.
  • Put the paytable on the machine. The cabinet shows every pay above the reels and lights the winning row, so a small 5x3 area sits inside a rich, always-informative object.
  • A sequel or a 'charged' version can be made with little new art: two extra words on the logo, 25 white lightning frames tinted cyan and a jackpot row carry the difference.
  • Build the environment from light instead of scenery: two mirrored ray pictures, a few white line pieces tinted in the game and eight pre-rendered views of one 3D sign give depth and constant movement with almost no painting.
  • Change one thing for the feature and change it completely: the ground flips from purple to orange and the blocks from purple to gold, while the cabinet stays, so the player never loses the board.
  • Keep an effect library in white and tint it per game: the flame frames here are the same files as in Fire Rail Express. Bake colour only where tint would flatten form (the gems).
  • For AI art work: the painted content is tiny (four fruits, one seven, one crown, one key-art card). The value is in the system around it, so the brief should fix the three hues and gold (#0b37b7 blue, #c366f7 purple, #c50b05 red, #f9c013 gold), the keyline-and-halo treatment and the slab lettering before any picture is made.

A toy-shop bank heist: glossy pink and gold piggy banks, candy bubble lettering and a steel vault with a pig's snout for a lock, set in a navy and gold bank hall, with a red-and-rainbow game-show wheel bolted on top as a shared feature.

  • #372e63 dark blue 10.3%
  • #683a50 magenta 9.5%
  • #f7f2e6 light orange 3.4%
  • #6509a3 purple 3.1%

Art direction Read

StyleGlossy cartoon with a soft 3D-look: fat, rounded, toy-like objects with no outlines, and thick outlined balloon lettering for every word. The pig is the only character and appears as symbol, mascot, lock, clasp, coin stamp and win-line head. The Super Wheel and the gamble wheel are flatter and more graphic, in a television game-show manner.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed gradients, a broad soft highlight and small hard white glints on every round form; gold is painted yellow-to-brown, not rendered. Backgrounds are clean stylised interiors in one-point perspective with detail kept at the vault door. Only the vault door's opening (31 frames) and the big-win gems read as true 3D renders.
ColourMeasured over the game's own art: mid-tone, saturated (59%), warm 52% against cool 40%, high contrast; the largest measured areas are the dark navy and plum grounds (#131025, #372e63, #683a50). On them sit three candy families: pig pink and magenta (#f676b7, #fe30a2), gold (#f4d020, #bc7d0b) and money green (#63b53e), with cyan (#08f9f1) behind pink pigs and feature tiles. Four prize colours are fixed everywhere: red Grand, purple Major, blue Minor, green Mini. The shared wheel adds its own red (#c90402).
LightingTop and top-left light on every object (measured: top 91, top-left 53, top-right 41 of the parts with a readable light side). Each symbol ships a 'Light' and a 'Light Hit' copy of itself as an additive layer for its flash, plus thin light sweeps. The hall is lit warm from windows and a ceiling lightbox against cool walls; the bonus room is lit by its own gold.
AmbienceFriendly greed: money as sweets and toys, nothing sinister about the bank. The base game is a calm night hall with a mascot watching from the top of the reels; the bonus is the inside of the vault, all gold. The shared Super Wheel brings a louder, studio-lights mood from outside the theme.
ShapesCircles and fat rounded squares: the pig is nearly a sphere, coins and wheels repeat it, tiles and panels have wide radii, letters are inflated. The snout (an oval with two holes) is the game's mark and is stamped on coins, bars, the case, the hammer, the vault and the carpet.
MaterialsGlazed ceramic, polished gold, paper banknotes, glossy plastic lettering, brushed steel for the vault, enamel wheels, cut gems.
TypographyAll display words are painted lettering (logo, WILD, COLLECT, BONUS, the win tiers, prize names). Running text and numbers are set by the client: 53 of its 82 text styles lead with Borsok and Alegreya Sans Black, in cream (#fffef0) with a navy stroke (#140d49) for the big-win title, as its text-style file states. Thirteen font files ship; the Helvetica, Tahoma, Roboto, Barlow and Arial Black ones serve the provider's interface (inference from the style lists).
MotionSkeletal: 64 Spine 3.8.99 skeletons, most of them short (0.83 s) bounce, win and collect moves on symbols built from a handful of parts, with longer idles for the mascot (4.17 s) and the scene (4.67 s). The signature move is the smash: a pig cracks, flies apart in 14 pre-cut shards and leaves a money heap. Frame sequences are kept for what a rig cannot do: the vault door (31 frames), spinning coins (18 a colour), gems (12 each), sparkles. The five intro pages are video clips. Curves in this Spine version are not read by the drawing tool, so the frames here show poses with linear easing.
VariantsPink to gold is the upgrade rule for every pig (symbol, pot pig, wheel pig). The cash pig exists at 1x1, 2x2, 3x3 and 4x3. Scenes, panels and logos ship in landscape and portrait versions inside one pack; base and bonus versions of the board, wheel and prize panels differ by backing and glow. Win words ship in six languages. The client serves the same art at 0.5 and 0.75 of the studio's size; this run holds the 0.75 pack.
ConstructionPixiJS client on Inspired's Virgo platform. 30 WebP atlas pages loaded of the 36 its manifest lists (the rest are other languages' win words and a US-CT wheel), up to 4096 px, packed by load order, not by subject, with trimmed and rotated frames listed in a packed manifest (base64 of LZ-UTF8 JSON), and all skeletons as JSON inside one data file. Symbols are small rigs of 4 to 30 parts with separate light layers; lettering is split into one sprite a letter where it must animate. Five of the pages are spent on the vault-door transition.
ConsistencyThe pig-and-money art is tight: one light, one finish, one lettering hand, one mark. The Super Wheel, its red interface and the gamble wheel are visibly a second system (flat fills, block capitals, red glow buttons), dressed with the logo and a snout coin but not redrawn in the toy style.

What to take from it Read

  • One mark carries a whole game: the snout is on at least nine different pieces, so plain objects (bars, a case, a coin) need no character art to belong.
  • Upgrade by material, not by new design: the same pig in pink then gold, at four sizes, gives the feature ladder with one character painted twice (small and large).
  • A breakable symbol is cheap when planned: paint the object once, cut 14 shards, add two crack overlays and a 'what is inside' picture.
  • Ship a 'Light' and a 'Light Hit' copy of each symbol as additive layers: win flashes then cost no new painting.
  • Fix a colour per prize (red, purple, blue, green) and repeat it on coins, panels, wheel wedges and flying tokens.
  • Keep the board near black and the scene dark navy so saturated symbols read; put scene detail where the reels do not cover it.
  • Budget texture memory for transitions: this game spends five 4096 px pages on one door opening. For AI art work, that sequence is a 3D render job, not an image-model job.
  • A shared platform feature (the Super Wheel) will look bolted on unless it is redrawn in the game's finish; here it was not, and it shows.

A sunny cruise-ship comedy about two rich pigs: a cream reel board in a thin gold frame on a white pool deck, five golden piggy banks above the reels waiting to crack, a chained blue Diamond Piggy over five enamel jackpot plates, and a night-club lounge kept for the bonus.

Art direction Read

StyleBright 3D-look cartoon in the manner of a family animation film, with caricature pigs as the stars (a cigar-and-cocktail tourist and a pin-up in sequins) and polished toy-like objects around them. The world is clean, new and expensive: white ship, blue pools, gold everywhere. One motif brands everything: the pig's snout, on the royals, the coin's back, the padlock, the clock and the flying tokens.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed volumes with hard cut edges for every object (soft edge: reel board 0.034, backdrops 0.034, jackpot plates 0.058, golden piggy banks 0.078, Ms. Piggy 0.086, high symbols 0.089, Mr. Piggy 0.125), flat-faceted crystal for the diamonds and the Diamond Piggy, and soft white light for every effect (bursts 0.909, rays 0.954). Lettering is flat two-tone with a thick outline.
ColourWhite, cream and pool blue as the ground, gold as the money, and saturated enamel colours for whatever must be told apart. Measured over the art files: near-white #f4f6f2 10% (the ship, the haze and white effect sprites), near-black violet #130616 9% (the lounge and outlines), gold-orange #eeb711 9%, grey #bbb8b6 8%, brown #7e3610 8%, blue #095cb9 5%, cream #f5ddb6 4%, dark blue #0e1557 3%. The board is the lightest large surface (cream #f5dbbd, brightness 0.84), which is rare for a slot: symbols are dark and saturated on a pale ground. Ice blue is reserved for the diamond (Wild, Diamond Piggy: 93% cool); a five-colour scale ranks the royals and, separately, the jackpot plates.
LightingHigh daylight: objects are lit from the top, top-left or top-right with warm red-orange core shadows and white glints, and a white haze is painted into the middle of the backdrop behind the board. The bonus lounge reverses it: a dark room with stage spots, pink and gold on the ceiling and cyan light from the crystal pig.
AmbienceCarefree, rich and a little cheeky: a luxury holiday where the only job is breaking piggy banks. Day on deck for the base game; a night version of the deck and a casino lounge for the features (the last two read from the files and the intro, not seen in play).
ShapesRound and fat throughout: piggy banks, coins, snouts, bellies, swim ring, fountain bowl, inflated letters. The counter-shapes are the hexagonal jackpot plates and the diamond's facets. Frames are thin and straight; nothing is ornate except the small gold leaf sprigs on the high-symbol tiles and the scrolls on the Wild.
MaterialsPolished gold, cut crystal, coloured enamel, pink skin, straw, printed cotton, sequins, pearls, leather, glass and liquid, tiled water, white painted steel, velvet and neon in the lounge.
TypographyFour voices. The logo: fat cartoon capitals, one colour per word (green, yellow, ice blue, pink) on a purple strip. Jackpot names and jackpot captions: black slab capitals with a gold rim. Feature captions and WILD: rounded yellow capitals with a dark violet outline. Win tiers: flared two-tone capitals in blue, magenta and yellow. Numbers are the provider's Ultra bitmap font, black with a gold rim on coins, plates and win amounts and cream with a wine outline on the progress counter; the low symbols are inflated letters with a snout. Small interface text is the shell's Poppins (Regular, SemiBold, Bold).
MotionAll rigged motion is Spine 4.2.43: 64 skeletons in one bundle file. The largest are Ms. Piggy (144 bones), Mr. Piggy (118), the breakable Diamond Piggy of the Smash & Win (100), the chained Diamond Piggy (93), the intro (81) and the feature splash (75). Beside them 23 frame sequences (496 frames): 232 frames of white glints that run over symbols, frames and the progress bar, 90 of a banknote and two diamonds turning, 83 of white bursts and reel anticipation, 61 of birds and window sparkle, 30 of the snout coin turning. Seen in play: reels of floating letters and framed props on the cream board; Golden Coins flipping on their axis to show a number, then throwing coins and snout tokens up at the golden piggy banks; stacked blue-diamond Wilds; a gold win line and the amount counting up in large black and gold numerals over a white-gold flash; the Piggy Progress number falling with each spin from 10 to 0; then FEATURE UNLOCKED, a golden card opening in a white flash with five reel-high Mr. Piggy figures that fly off it onto the reels, and the counter starting again at 25. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7.
VariantsThree scenes from three half pictures: the deck by day (normal), the deck by night (special) and the lounge (the Smash & Win and the intro); rigs carry skins normal, special and bonus. Each golden piggy bank exists in 18 paintings (six stages of cracking in three looks). Two pigs as full-reel figures, as portrait tiles in the paytable and as heads on the logo. Five jackpot plates from one shape in five colours; four Jackpot Coin faces from one coin. Landscape and portrait skins for logo, counter and positions (only landscape at 1280x720 was captured).
ConstructionTwo packed 4096 px atlas pages hold 819 sprites, 496 of them animation frames, with 13 localised lettering files (en-GB), five loose textures and one skeleton bundle. Backdrops ship as the left half of a symmetric scene (1034x1885), with the middle washed to white where the board covers it. Characters and high symbols are layered cut-outs on bones; coins are front, back and side pictures flipped by a rig; the Diamond Piggy of the bonus is literally its 14 breakable pieces. Every glint and burst is a white sprite or sequence tinted in the game. Paytable pictures, the flattened logo, the numeral fonts and the interface come from the provider's shared services.
ConsistencyHigh. Gold settings, the snout motif and the same top-lit airbrushed finish run from the backdrop to the smallest token, and the pigs' pink and the diamond's blue are kept off everything else. Seams: the win-tier lettering and the yellow captions are flatter and more generic than the painted world; the white birds are plain silhouettes; and the caricature pigs are drawn with more grit (cigar, stubble, heavy make-up) than the toy-like piggy banks beside them.

What to take from it Read

  • Put the game's long-term goal on screen as an object. The chained Diamond Piggy, the pocket-watch counter and the five golden banks are the whole top third of the base game: the player sees what is locked, how far it is and what each reel is building towards, before reading a word.
  • Paint anticipation, not only results. One golden piggy bank is painted 18 times (six stages of cracks in three looks) although, as the rules state, the cracks do not change the odds. That is where this game spends its illustration budget, and it is a kind of work image generation does well: one object, many controlled states.
  • A pale board is possible. Cream #f5dbbd under dark, saturated symbols reads cleanly and makes the game look unlike the dark-cabinet slots around it; high symbols bring their own coloured tile, low symbols float.
  • Theme the royals with one detail. A snout worked into 10, J, Q, K and A, plus an 18-frame white glint each, makes the cheapest symbols belong to the game with five pictures.
  • Reserve one colour for the prize. Ice blue appears only on the diamond Wild, the falling diamonds and the Diamond Piggy, so the screen's one cold object is the thing to want.
  • Build breakable things from their pieces. The bonus pig is 14 shell pieces and 10 blurred shards assembled into a whole; breaking it needs no extra drawing. For our packages: when an object must break, generate it whole, then cut it.
  • Half a backdrop is enough when the board sits in the middle: each scene is one 1034x1885 picture for the left side, mirrored (by inference) for the right, with the centre left as haze.
  • Two-sided flat objects flipped by a rig (coin face, snout back, edge disc) give a 3D turn for three pictures; drawn frames are kept for what bones cannot do (a tumbling banknote, a turning gem, glints).
  • Characters double as symbols and presenters: each pig is one large rig (118 and 144 bones) used as the full-reel Collector, in the intro, and, by its animation names, in the big-win scene. Design the character at reel height first.
  • From the same provider and framework as the six earlier Octoplay runs (same shell, Poppins, Double Chance card, Ultra numerals, one skeleton bundle in Spine 4.2.43, packed 4096 px pages), and by the provider's own description a sequel ('The pigs are back'): the framework is constant, and the art budget moves into characters and into a persistent unlock structure, here four levels over 10, 25, 50 and 75 spins.

Art direction Read

StyleCasino-floor object illustration, carried over from a land-based cabinet (inference from the cabinet-style signage, credit-based pays and bet-level buttons). Everything is a thing of wealth shown as an icon: vault door, diamond, gold bars, banknotes, coins, money bag, currency signs, card letters. The setting is an abstract banknote pattern, not a scene; the only place the game ever shows is the gold-ringed vault chamber of the bonus.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed gradients, hard silhouettes and bright specular streaks; 12% of edges measure soft over the whole game. High symbols sit on a rounded tile of their own colour; low symbols are bevelled letters with a white edge and a black outline. Titles are extruded, bevelled display lettering. Lightning is the one soft, glowing family (77% soft edges).
ColourGreen, gold and black, with blue as the charge. Measured over the game's own art: black #060f09 33%, black-teal #0e3e2f 10%, orange-gold #e79510 10%, white #f3f9f8 5%, dark green #0d6d06 4%, blue #0366f6 3%, green #06a04b 2%; saturation 0.67, warm 39% against cool 41%; hues green 31%, orange 22%, blue 13%, yellow 12%. The base background is two greens only (#046c31, #04af53). Each high symbol owns a tile colour (diamond red, gold bars blue, notes purple, coins dark green) and each letter one flat colour (A red, K blue, Q yellow, J green). The free spins swap the field to red (#ce110a). Jackpot tiers: Grand red, Major green, Minor blue, Mini purple. Lightning is #0269f7 with a white core.
LightingA plain light from above on nearly everything (top on 354 parts measured, top-right 81, top-left 55), with white streak highlights on gold. No scene lighting, no cast light between objects. Lightning and the vault symbol's landing flash are self-lit.
AmbienceBright, clean and blunt: the promise is money itself. Calm in the base game, hotter by colour alone in the free spins, and charged when the lightning locks the green discs in the bonus.
ShapesRound and heavy: discs, coins, the vault wheel, the sack, the ring of the vault chamber. Rounded square tiles for high symbols. Slab-serif letters. The background's only ornament is banknote engraving: guilloche curves and scrollwork.
MaterialsPolished gold above all; cut diamond; printed paper money; enamel-coloured letters; black glass panels with hairline rainbow edges and gold corner beads; a dark neutral plastic for the console.
TypographyThe logo is gold slab-serif capitals on two arches with a red-brown extrusion and a laurel; MONEY CHARGE is white-violet italic capitals over yellow JACKPOTS on a purple extrusion; WILD is cream western slab lettering; the disc values are cream slab numerals baked into each picture. Help pages set live text in red-orange outlined serif small capitals. 25 font files are embedded (among them Cinzel, Alfa Slab One, Bodoni, Trajan Pro, Bebas Neue, Roboto, Myriad Pro, Dollar Bill); which of them this game draws with was not traced, and a list this long reads as a provider's shared set (inference).
MotionFrame sequences only: no skeleton and no Spine file is shipped, so the empty assembled folder says nothing more than that. 45 sequences hold 854 frames: every symbol has a pre-rendered win animation (14 frames for the diamond, 24 for the other high symbols, 38 for each low symbol), the wild and the vault also a landing animation, the vault door swings open in 50 frames, lightning runs in 14 looping sets (276 frames, the largest), and coins and gems tumble in 24 frames each for the big win. Symbols mostly stay in place while a highlight crosses them; the energy comes from flashes and lightning, not from deforming art.
VariantsEvery symbol in three states: still, dimmed copy (drawn, about a quarter as bright) and animation. The Money Charge disc in 29 baked values, lit and dimmed. Reel window with a green or a red edge; background in green, red, paytable and loading versions. Titles with and without the word JACKPOTS, for markets without the jackpot. Only the desktop landscape layout was captured; the files name portrait cuts as well.
Construction29 texture pages, 1,188 named sprites in TexturePacker atlases, one atlas per symbol animation and one per screen (base game, preloader, paytable, vault gateway, Money Charge, menus, autoplay). Backgrounds are four JPEGs at 1440x810. Everything is a bitmap or a frame sequence; values and pay rows are baked pictures; labels and meters are live text. The console and the autoplay panel are a neutral dark kit that is not themed to the game.
ConsistencyVery consistent and very narrow: one rendering manner for every object, one green for the world, gold for value, blue lightning for the feature. The console is the one foreign body, grey-violet and unthemed. The feature's brand (Money Charge Jackpots, violet and yellow) deliberately does not match the game's green and gold, so it reads as a badge shared across games (inference).

What to take from it Read

  • A leading US online slot can carry no character, no world and no story: this one ranks on thirteen clear money icons, a jackpot panel and one feature effect. Clarity of symbols on black beats scenery here.
  • The black reel window with a coloured tile behind each high symbol is a cheap, strong recipe for legibility: every symbol is identifiable by colour alone at thumbnail size.
  • One effect family, used everywhere, gives the feature its identity: blue lightning frames the meters, the title, each locked symbol and the total. It is the only cold colour in the game, so it never competes with the art.
  • Production is frame sequences and stills only, with no rigging: 854 frames, most of them a highlight crossing a still picture. This is art an image pipeline can produce directly: a still per symbol, a dimmed copy, and a short shine or flash sequence.
  • Feature variants are done by recolour, not new art: the free spins are the same background in red and the same reel window with a red edge.
  • Values baked into pictures (29 discs, twice) cost sprites but guarantee the look of the numerals; live text is kept for meters and rules.
  • The loading screen sells the three features as three captioned cards before play; it is the clearest statement of what the game wants the player to hope for.

Art direction Read

StyleThree manners side by side. The regular symbols are stylised, glossy, toy-like objects with a gold rim and small engraved spirals. The fireball, the flames and the win effects are photographic fire. The wild is a realistic painted pin-up figure in an Aztec or Maya costume. The setting is 3D-rendered stone architecture; the bonus backdrop is a flatter, posterised painting of a volcano.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed gradients with hard silhouettes, a gold outline, one white star glint and a drop shadow on every regular symbol. Frames and panels are flat fretwork ornament with no depth. Fire is soft and bright with sharp embers. Nothing has a drawn black outline except the flat black value digits on the fireballs.
ColourRed, black and gold, with teal as the single counter-colour. Measured over the game's own art, the palette is led by near-black #170507, dark red #5c0d0f and red #9b130f and #ee2509, then orange #ed9e1c and gold #f7dd5b; saturation 80%, warm 87% against cool 9%. The reel cells are teal (#07998e, #036156) in the base game, so the board separates from the red hall (#a31d05); in the free spins the cells turn red (#9b0108) and the hall brighter red (#f52205). The bonus adds magenta (#7e072a and a 19% magenta share of hues). Each fruit owns one hue. The four prize tiers own one flat text colour each: red Grand, pink Major (#fb67b1), green Minor (#32fa64), cyan Mini (#31c6f7). The spin button is green.
LightingFire is the light everywhere: the hall is lit from below and in front as if by firelight, the fireball and flames are self-lit, the wild is lit warm from the fire behind her. The regular symbols alone have a neutral studio light from the upper left with a star glint.
AmbienceHot, enclosed and ceremonial in the base game; hotter in the free spins; vast and ominous in the bonus, under a red spiral sky. Over it sits the plain cheer of a classic fruit machine: the theme is a dressing on familiar symbols, not a story.
ShapesRound, full, simple silhouettes for the symbols; rectangles and thin rails for every frame; the step-fret (a squared spiral) as the one ornament, repeated on frames, button rings, the coin, the ribbon ends, the cell pattern and even the watermelon seeds.
MaterialsGlossy fruit skin, enamel and polished gold; rough cut stone; gold fretwork; glass-dome buttons; feathers, turquoise and gold jewellery on the wild; molten rock, flame and embers.
TypographyThe logo is heavy slab-serif capitals with a yellow-to-red gradient, a flame texture and a dark red extrusion; FREE SPINS and WILD are drawn in the same bevelled manner. Everything else is live text in Oswald (Bold, Regular and Light are embedded): condensed capitals in yellow or peach for labels and figures, and flat tier colours for the prize meters. The values on the fireballs are a black condensed bitmap font with an orange edge, in two sizes.
MotionNo skeletons: the game's own art is animated as Flash-style timelines at 30 frames a second (the files call them view-builder animations) over still pictures, with short frame sequences for fire. A winning symbol gets an outline glow, a spark and a looping 30-frame flame; the fireball boils over 30 frames; the Free Spins volcano throws lava in 30 frames over three stills of rising brightness; the full-reel wild moves only her headdress (13 frames), lips, brows and earrings, with two 27-frame flames at her hands. On a win every symbol off the line is dimmed and the winning cells get a sparkling frame, with the line amount in a small black box. Anticipation is a six-frame burning outline around a reel or a cell. Coins on a win are a particle emitter over a six-frame coin. The four Spine 4.1.24 skeletons among the captured files belong to a promotional overlay of the demo's host (a vault and raccoon theme), not to this game.
VariantsOne hall in two brightnesses (base and free spins) and one separate bonus scene, which is also the loading picture. Reel backing in teal and red. Each symbol in three forms: a reel picture, a small paytable copy and a layered win version. In the free spins the three middle reels are linked and show one giant symbol, the same reel picture at three cells high. The fireball as a blank ball, with a live value, and with Mini, Minor or Major lettering. The wild as a one-cell bust and a three-cell standing figure. One button family (gold fret ring with a glass dome) in green, yellow, blue and red, each with lit and grey states.
Construction621 named sprites on 67 textures, of which 56 units are the game's own art; 362 of the sprites are frames of 32 sequences. Sheets are in IGT's own view-builder format (a JSON of named sprites with frame rectangles beside each PNG, and a timeline file). Reel symbols are 558x500 pictures for a 261x238 cell. Backgrounds are single 1920x1080 JPEGs with no layers. The flame frames are repeated on each symbol sheet. Large light effects are small (the impact explosion is 96x96) and scaled up.
ConsistencyTight in colour and ornament, loose in manner. The red-gold-teal palette and the step-fret hold everything together, which lets three rendering styles (toy fruit, photographic fire, pin-up figure) sit on one board. The bonus backdrop is the one piece in a different hand: flat and posterised against the rendered hall.

What to take from it Read

  • The top-ranked game of the report is visually modest: stills, flat frames and short frame loops, with no rigged character and no layered background. Its strength is clarity, not production volume.
  • One counter-colour does the layout work. A teal board in a red room, and a green spin button on a red and gold screen, separate play area and main control without size or decoration.
  • The feature symbol is told apart by manner, not by a frame or a badge: a realistic burning ball among glossy toy fruit. Black flat digits on it stay readable on the brightest object of the board.
  • Mode changes are cheap and clear: the free spins are the same hall and board pushed to red; the bonus swaps the backdrop and dims every symbol that is not a fireball. The free spins reuse the reel pictures at three times the size as giant symbols, which is why they are shipped at 558x500.
  • One ornament (the step-fret) repeated on every frame, button, coin and ribbon is enough to theme a set of otherwise generic classic symbols.
  • A full-height character is made to feel alive with four small moving pieces and two flame loops over a still painting. For AI-made art this is a reachable target: a strong still plus a few cut pieces, rather than a full rig.
  • Each win version is the reel picture plus three shared layers (outline glow, spark, flame loop). A symbol set built this way needs one good still per symbol and one shared effects kit.

A land-based classic kept almost as it was: a gold and red-lacquer Egyptian shrine of 5x3 reels on a one-colour purple dusk, gold-and-enamel symbols each on its own coloured cloth, and a single face, Cleopatra's green eyes under a jewelled headdress, as key art, logo and wild.

Art direction Read

StyleCasino cabinet glass art: comic-style glamour illustration with hard outlines for Cleopatra and the logo, airbrushed gold-and-enamel objects for the picture symbols, gold Art Nouveau letters with lotus buds for the card ranks, and a flat poster-like Sphinx for the scatter. The cabinet and plaques are cleaner, smoother illustration; the backdrop is a one-hue tinted photo-based picture (inference); the one fire effect is naturalistic.
RenderingHard-edged throughout (soft edge 0.05 over the game's art), smooth airbrushed gradients inside thin dark outlines, white streak highlights on gold, a woven texture on the symbol cloths and a fibre texture on the free-spin papyrus. Everything is a flat finished picture: nothing is layered or lit by the scene.
ColourGold on purple. Measured over the game's own art the palette is gold #f0c70a (15%), orange #de7f25 (13%), near-black #120a04, sand #eeca79, brown #67370a, red #861425 and cream #f9e9bc; saturation 0.76, warm 90% against cool 6%. The backdrop is the counter-colour, magenta #9d1cae and purple #6a0cca in the base game, and turns dark red #880d30 in the free spins. The reel cells are cream #f8e6bf in the base game and tan #e8c684 in the free spins. Each picture symbol owns a cloth colour (scarab green #3a8467, lotus violet #753e7e, cartouche blue #3f55b1, crook and flail yellow #e8ad1e, eye red #b92911) and each of the 20 paylines owns a bead colour that its line and cell frames repeat.
LightingNo scene lighting. Each object carries its own frontal highlight; the cabinet has banded reflections like polished metal; the Sphinx (scatter and Big Win) and the fire are self-lit. The backdrop is a plain vertical gradient with no sun or lamp.
AmbienceOpulent, calm and familiar: a jewel box at dusk. The base game is cool purple around warm gold; the free spins heat the whole screen to crimson and age the reels to tan papyrus. Nothing moves until a win, so the game feels like a machine rather than a scene.
ShapesSquare opaque cells in a strict grid; a symmetrical shrine frame with a curved cornice, two lotus columns and a boat-shaped base with fan prows; round beads and round buttons; the lotus fan as the repeating ornament (on the letters, the logo, the cabinet, the plaque).
MaterialsPolished gold, blue and turquoise enamel, cut gems, red lacquer, woven cloth, cream paper and tan papyrus, sandstone, glass beads and glass-dome buttons, fire.
TypographyThe wordmark is drawn: red capitals with a yellow inner line, a blue band and a gold rim, the C and the R enlarged, in the same comic manner as the face. The words on symbols (SCATTER, BONUS, DOUBLE) are fat cartoon capitals in red-to-yellow or red on violet. Everything else is live text in two embedded sans-serif fonts, Lato Bold and Roboto Regular: yellow for the free-spin messages, blue capitals for BIG WIN, white amounts, orange labels and green win figures on the meter bar. The paytable is a plain white web page with a blue-headed table.
MotionNo skeletons and no timelines in the files: all animation is frame by frame, as full pictures. The wild has an 80-frame sequence in which the cell turns gold and two hands cross and open over the logo plate to show DOUBLE (and a second 80-frame version that keeps the logo); the Sphinx has 40-frame sequences in which the face glows, flames rise and SCATTER or BONUS wipes in; the Big Win is a 40-frame glow pulse of a Sphinx over a plaque with a counting number; the transition into and out of the free spins is 32 frames of fire inside a gold frame on black; a payline bead gets a 30-frame sparkle. The regular symbols do not animate: a win greys every other cell, frames the winning cells in the line's colour, draws the line to its bead and shows the amount in a small black tag (seen on the screens). The backdrop and cabinet never move.
VariantsTwo modes made by recolour: backdrop purple or crimson, cabinet window cream or tan, every symbol on a cream or tan ground, and each animated sequence shipped once per ground. Scatter in two words (SCATTER, BONUS), wild in two plates (DOUBLE, Cleopatra). Twenty bead colours and a grey. Buttons in four states. The client ships a desktop pack (symbols 244x244, backdrop 1920x1080, read here) and a mobile pack with the same art at half size in fewer atlases (symbols 122x122; captured first by mistake, see the record).
ConstructionA small package: 19 textures, 705 named sprites, 14 frame sequences with 611 frames, 2 fonts. Every atlas is a TexturePacker JSON with the studio's own names. Symbols are untrimmed opaque 244x244 cells with the ground baked in; the cabinet is one 1645x1080 picture per mode with the window painted in and a divider grid laid over the symbols; the backdrop is one mirrored JPEG per mode. Mode differences are made by whole second copies, not by layers or tints: 320 of the 611 animation frames are the wild, and half of all animation frames exist only to change a cell margin from cream to tan. Text is live, so the art holds no language.
ConsistencyThe identity is tight where it matters: one face and one wordmark serve as key art, logo and wild, and gold with lotus ornament runs through symbols, cabinet and plaques. Around that the manners differ openly: outlined comic face, airbrushed objects, flat Sphinx, smooth vector-like cabinet, tinted photo backdrop, naturalistic fire, and generic blue and red web buttons for autospin. The game reads as one because of its strict grid, its gold and its single counter-colour, not because the rendering is uniform.

What to take from it Read

  • A top-20 game in this report runs on 19 textures and frame-by-frame art with no skeletons, no particles and a backdrop that never moves: at this end of the market, recognition and readability outweigh production depth. Inference: its rank rests on the brand's long history, not on the art's finish.
  • One colour per symbol. Each picture symbol sits on its own cloth colour and each rank has its own inlay, so the board is read by colour before shape; worth copying in any dense 5x3 set.
  • One key image used three ways (loading picture, logo, wild) gives a simple game a strong face. Plan the wild, the logo and the key art as one drawing.
  • The rule is shown on the symbol: the wild's plate changes to DOUBLE when it doubles a win, and the scatter writes SCATTER or BONUS on itself. Stating the mechanic in the art, at the point the player is looking, replaces a popup.
  • A feature mode from recolour alone: backdrop hue, cell ground and meter bar change, nothing else. It is cheap and it reads at once; with layered symbols and a tint it would cost a fraction of the copies shipped here.
  • Payline colour as the win language (bead, line and cell frame in one colour, everything else greyed) is clear with one line and gets muddy with several close colours; a modern version would keep the idea with fewer, better separated colours.
  • For AI art work: the set is a clean reference for 'classic land-based Egyptian' as a style target (gold and enamel objects on coloured cloth, Art Nouveau gold letters, comic glamour face), and its flat, unlayered cells are easy to match piece for piece in a concept.

Art direction Read

StyleGlossy casino illustration with a 3D-rendered look for the train, coins and symbols, set against graphic paper ephemera (postcards and tickets printed with engravings) and Wild West poster lettering. The reel board itself is restrained Art Deco.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed volumes, pinpoint highlights and hard outer edges on every object; soft additive glows and cartoon fire for effects. Symbols carry a warm rim light so they sit in the fire's glow.
ColourGold and fire against purple. Measured over the game's art: near-black #240d0f 26%, orange #e9800f 13%, dark purple #431a56 11%, brown #804309 11%, gold #f6c723 6%, light gold #fdfcf7 4%, dark red #740505 3%. The four jackpots own purple (MINI), blue (MINOR), green (MAJOR) and red (GRAND), repeated on coin, plaque and win word; the three win tiers are purple, blue and red. The amounts are purple numerals with a gold rim. Steel grey appears once, on the horseshoe.
LightingObjects are lit from the upper left or front with a red-orange rim from below right; the backdrop's fire lights from the bottom of the screen. Lamps, coins' flames and all effects are self-lit.
AmbienceA furnace and a ticket office: hot, rich, a little nostalgic. The base game is half fire and half cool purple; the cash bonus turns the backdrop to gold and purple postcards, the jackpot bonus to fire across the whole screen.
ShapesCircles (coins, wheel, boiler door, fire rings), the perforated ticket rectangle, rounded plaques with one cut corner, a thin square frame, fat slab-serif letters.
MaterialsPolished gold, lacquered purple steel, enamel, copper, steel, fruit skin, worn printed card, fire, steam.
TypographyDrawn lettering in one family of Western slab serifs: black on gold for the logo, fire-filled for WILD, coloured enamel for the jackpot words, purple, blue and red with gold outlines for the win tiers, cream with a red edge for the splash sentences. One bitmap numeral font, purple with a gold rim. Everything else is the provider shell's Poppins (Regular, SemiBold, Bold).
MotionAll motion is Spine 4.2.43: 41 skeletons in one file, most of them scene layers and effects, moving still pictures and 25 hand-drawn frame sequences (445 frames: fire, glints, a turning coin and ticket). The train is one picture with animated wheel, rods, highlights and sparks. Seen in play: a fire sweep after START, coins thrown on the pile, the train driving across the reels into the bonus, coin and ticket showers, fire inside the live jackpot frame. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7.
VariantsThree backdrop states (base, cash bonus, jackpot bonus), two reel boards, six coin faces from one blank, two collectors from one train, two splash cards, three win tiers from one layout, fruit symbols from one fruit each with darker side copies.
ConstructionThree 4096 px atlas pages hold 532 sprites; backdrops are tall columns, the board and frames are mirrored halves, flames ship white to be tinted, words are separate from the coins and plaques they sit on. Five localised lettering files (en-GB). Paytable and buy-card pictures, the numeral font and the interface come from the provider's shared services.
ConsistencyHigh. Gold, the flame emblem and the slab serif recur on every piece, and the ticket shape returns as logo, particle and backdrop. The one seam is between the rendered-look objects and the flat engraved postcards, and it is used on purpose as foreground against background.

What to take from it Read

  • One hero object can carry a game: the train is a single picture, and highlights, sparks, a blurred wheel and a coin pile make it feel alive. Budget the render, not the rig.
  • Colour-code the prizes end to end: each jackpot keeps its colour on the coin, the plaque and the win word, so a 3x3 board reads at a glance.
  • A classic fruit set is made new by context, not by redrawing fruit: rim light from the fire, three-of-a-kind clusters built from one painted fruit and a darker copy.
  • Split the backdrop into two contrasting halves (hot painted fire, cool printed paper) and swap them per feature: three moods from four narrow pictures.
  • Ship fire and light in white and tint in the game: one flame sequence serves every jackpot colour. Useful for AI-made effects too, where consistent colour across frames is hard.
  • Keep words apart from the objects they label (coins, plaques, splashes): localisation touches five files only.
  • For AI art work: the painted pieces are few and still; the craft is in consistency of gold, rim light and lettering, which is where a style reference and a fixed palette (#f6c723 gold, #431a56 purple, #e9800f fire) should be set.

A cartoon Frankenstein laboratory lit by acid-green electricity: a child-like monster mascot, chunky lab hardware in teal and copper, plasma-ball prizes in neon colours, and gold kept for money.

Art direction Read

StyleFamily-animation cartoon horror with a 3D-look painted finish. Frankie and the Bride have big heads, heavy lids and small bodies; props (hand, ray gun, control box, brain jars, specimen jars) are rounded and toy-like. Nothing is gory: stitches, bolts, brains and eyeballs are played as sweets and toys. Lettering is horror-comic: dripping green words and fat gold slabs.
RenderingSmooth gradients, clean hard silhouettes, no line outlines (measured: 5% soft edge over the game's art). Detail and gloss are spent on the symbols, the jars and Frankie; backgrounds are hazy paintings kept empty in the middle. Every glow, arc and burst is a separate layer on black, added on top.
ColourMeasured over the game's own art: vivid (saturation 78%), mid-to-dark (brightness 36%), cool 63% against warm 12%. Black-green #0d1610 26%, dark green #296909 17%, dark blue #112e45 9%, teal #0b887d 8%, bright green #38b512 4%, purple #3b126f 3%; green is 52% of the coloured pixels. The scheme: teal fog and violet shadow for the room, acid green for electricity and light, copper for the frame, and gold with a red edge only for money (cash balls, win numerals, COLLECT). Three bonus games are told apart by colour alone, red, green and blue, and four jackpots by green, blue, magenta and red.
LightingLight comes from the things in the picture: electrode balls, plasma, liquid in jars, lightning, the storm sky. Objects are top-lit (measured: light from the top on 163 parts, top-left and top-right on about 50 each) with a coloured glow behind them. The reel backing is unlit black, so everything luminous reads against it.
AmbienceSpooky but cosy and funny: a Halloween cartoon, with the machine always humming. The base game is the lab at night; Cash Trail goes outside to the stormy hill and castle; Big Money is a shelf of specimen jars; Frankie Spins darkens the lab and lights only the prizes.
ShapesRound and chunky: cylinders, domes, balls and fat letters. The angular shapes are lightning, thorny vines and bare trees, used for energy and for the outdoors. Frames are copper pipe or thin gold; the Collect symbol breaks the grid with a vine border.
MaterialsGreen enamelled metal, copper pipe and brass bolts, glass with coloured liquid and bubbles, plasma behind glass, stitched green skin, cloth, cork, aged wood, gold lettering and coins.
TypographyDisplay lettering is drawn art: green condensed capitals and a gold slab for the logo, dripping slime letters for WILD and IT'S ALIVE!, green slab words with a blue or dark edge for win tiers and bonus words, fat outlined words for the jackpots. Eight bitmap numeral fonts in one rounded design (gold and red for money, white for counters, teal for totals). Running text is the shell's Roboto.
MotionSpine carries everything: 73 skeletons, 71 of them made in Spine 4.2.43 (six exported as 4.1; the two Power Play rigs are 3.8), from 3-bone symbol pulses (land 0.67 s, win 1.0 s) to Frankie's 138-bone expanded symbol and the 108-bone Mega Frankie. Electricity is hand-made frame sequences played inside the rigs: 61 sequences, 891 frames (arcs of 30 frames, plasma of 21, lightning of 23, win boxes of 30). Hands change pose by swapping numbered pictures. No skeleton frame is drawn in this report: the tools cannot draw Spine 4.2, so motion is read from the files and the screens.
VariantsOne design, several colours, is the rule: three brain jars, four jackpot balls, four specimen jars, jar counters in red and blue. Each paying symbol ships as a still, a win copy, a painted blur and, for Frankie Spins, a dimmed green copy and its blur at a smaller cell size. Frankie exists as a Collect tile, an expanded three-cell figure, a 2x2 to 5x5 Mega Frankie and a figure for intros. Intro screens and the trail have separate portrait rigs and, for the trail, a separate portrait painting.
Construction1,679 named pictures from 1,233 files. Almost all art is loose PNG and JPEG files in folders named by use, with Spine JSON beside them; only the three brain jars, Mega Frankie and the level meter are packed Spine atlases. Files with words in them end in _ml, one set per language (inference from the naming). Effects are JPEG on black for additive slots. The base game loads first; each bonus game's art (373 more files) loads only when that bonus starts.
ConsistencyTight: one character design, one hardware family, one green. What sits outside is the Power Play and bonus wheel set, in a chrome blue and gold style with a 'Super Mode' logo placeholder, which looks like a shared template of the provider (inference; listed under the provider's interface and not read), and the big win's coins and gems, which are generic.

What to take from it Read

  • The build read here is Blueprint Gaming's (BP_FrankensteinsFortune95), not the White Hat Studios US build the market report ranks; treat every finding as about this title's art, with the match between the two builds as inference.
  • One light source idea runs the whole game: green electricity. Arcs on the frame, win boxes, the modifier frame, plasma prizes and lightning in the jars are all the same few hand-made frame sequences, recoloured and reused.
  • Colour is the navigation: red, green and blue name the three bonus games on the meters, the symbols, the counters and the result screens, and gold is reserved for money. An artist's brief for a similar game can fix this palette logic before any asset is drawn.
  • Progress is always a physical object filling up (a brain jar, a glass tube), never an abstract bar. The jar rig, with six liquid levels, is drawn once and coloured three times.
  • The mascot is one set of about 60 body parts reused in five rigs (symbol, expanded symbol, Mega Frankie, modifier walk-on, intros). The cost is in rigging and hand poses, not in new paintings: a generated character still needs to be cut into parts like these.
  • Scene art is not economised: four full paintings at 3200x3200 (the lab, its congratulations copy, the trail in landscape and in portrait) and four more at 1600x1600, each empty where the board or the prizes sit.
  • Dimming losers instead of removing them (the green 'off' symbol set of Frankie Spins) keeps a hold-and-collect board full and on-theme for the price of one recolour per symbol.

An American-anniversary slot dressed as a prize ceremony: a 3x3 glass board hung with bunting in front of a flag made of light, gold medals for every prize, three smiling presidents as collectors, and a Statue of Liberty that turns to gold coin by coin.

Art direction Read

StyleGlossy realistic casino illustration with a sticker finish. Objects, medals and portraits are fully painted and idealised; the backdrop is flat graphic design. The portraits are warm caricature, close to animated-film character design, while the emblems and the statue stay realistic.
RenderingThree kinds. Painted objects with smooth blended volume, fine detail and hard outer edges (emblems soft edge 0.147, jackpot coins 0.121, help pictures 0.037), each pay symbol on a thick white outline. Flat gradients for the backdrop and the board panel. White light sprites with feathered edges, tinted and added by the game (glows 0.898, sparks 0.88, fireworks 0.909). Lettering is extruded with a lighter upper band, a gold keyline and a navy or dark red block shadow.
ColourRed, white and blue hold the stage; gold holds everything that pays. Measured over the art files: orange-gold #d7911e 12%, near-white #fbfaf5 11%, dark red #56090a 10%, red #a01c1b 9%, blue #2d78c2 8%, near-black navy #0d1830 8%, gold #f4c64a 4%, light blue #76bae6 3%. The backdrop is half navy, half red (hues blue 0.518, red 0.482); the board is pale sky blue so the warm symbols stand out. A second code names the prizes: purple Unity, blue Justice, green Freedom, red Glory, and the win tiers borrow those colours (magenta BIG, green SUPER, gold MEGA, blue TOTAL). Gold against full colour separates cash from jackpot: the Cash Collector and its coins are all gold, the Jackpot Collectors are in natural colour.
LightingBright, even studio light from above and the upper left on every object, with small white hot spots on metal; no cast shadows between pieces except the drop shadows painted into the bunting and scroll. The backdrop glows from its centre behind the board and is the darkest layer (brightness 0.254), the symbols the brightest.
AmbienceA Fourth of July parade and an awards ceremony at once: festive, proud, polished, without irony. Fireworks open the game and confetti never stops.
ShapesThe five-point star (backdrop, medals, ribbons, the empty cell, the flying coin), the round medal, the scroll ribbon with curled ends, the laurel branch, and the stripe. The board is a plain rounded rectangle so the round and ribboned shapes read against it.
MaterialsPolished gold above all (coins, medals, ribbons, laurels, the gilded statue), then satin bunting and flags, coloured glass domes, enamel lettering, parchment, feather, brass and wood, plumage, painted skin and cloth in the portraits, and weathered blue-grey metal for the statue before it is gilded.
TypographyHeavy sans capitals throughout. The logo sets FREEDOM upright in red and 250x BOOST and HOLD AND WIN slanted in blue and white, all with a gold keyline and navy block shadow. Jackpot names are arched on ribbons in their own colours. Numbers come from a provider bitmap font (the service calls it MyriadPro): white rounded numerals with a glowing gold keyline and dark red shadow. The words on collectors (CASH, JACKPOT, COLLECTOR) are sprites, the splash sentences are localised picture files, and small interface text is the provider shell's Poppins (Regular, SemiBold, Bold).
MotionAll motion is Spine 4.2.43: 43 skeletons in one bundle, moving, scaling, tinting and mesh-bending still pictures, plus 25 hand-drawn frame sequences (426 frames). Twenty-one of the sequences are white highlight sweeps drawn to the shape of one symbol layer; the others are the turning star coin, tumbling confetti and two spark animations. Seen in play: fireworks over the board as the intro gives way to the game; confetti drifting all the time; symbols blurring vertically on the reels; a Golden Coin throwing star coins up to the statue, whose gold rises a band at a time; a Jackpot Coin throwing a coin to the jackpot medallions, which flip; a gold ribbon unrolling across the board with the collected amount and a burst of coins; a thin gold line through a paying row with the winning symbols flaring white; a reel lit by a column of yellow-white light as a coin lands; the Jackpot Hold & Win, where the base game washes red under a BONUS GAME splash, fireworks and puffs of red, white and blue smoke cover the change, the backdrop and board turn red with a gold star in each empty cell and a red 1 2 3 ribbon in place of the logo, and a collected jackpot fills the screen with CONGRATS!, its medal on a purple glow, the amount and a shower of star coins; and the end of that bonus, where the sum leaves the collector, counts up on the gold ribbon over blue rays and MEGA WIN arrives in gold between two laurels under an arc of stars. The collectors' faces are rigged to blink and move (109 bones), read from the file. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7.
VariantsThree stage states from one set of parts by skin: normal (navy and red backdrop, pale blue board), bonus (all red, seen in the Jackpot Hold & Win) and special (all blue, the cash Hold & Win, seen only in the picture of the help page), each bonus with a respin ribbon in its colour. Four jackpot medals as recolours of one painting, at symbol size and again at win-screen size. One medallion kit for four collectors, gold for cash and full colour for jackpot. The statue in blue-grey and in gold. Every effect in white, tinted per use. Only the 1280x720 landscape layout was captured.
ConstructionTwo atlas pages (4096x4096 and 4096x2477) hold 615 sprites, 426 of them animation frames; three backdrop pictures take about 30% of the first page. The board panel, the bunting and the flags are half-pieces mirrored by the rig. Symbols are layered (back, front, white outline, star, sweep). The statue's gilding is thirty rising bands of a gold repaint revealed by the rig. Six localised lettering files (en-GB), nineteen help pictures and a help logo from the provider's paytable service, the numeral font from its font service, six small shared helper textures.
ConsistencyHigh. One gold, one star, one ribbon shape and one lettering construction run through logo, board, symbols, prizes and win screens, and the statue appears three times (scene figure, gilded figure, Cash Collector). The seams are small: the caricature presidents are in a lighter register than the realistic emblems, and the flat graphic backdrop is a different kind of picture from everything in front of it, which is what lets it sit back.

What to take from it Read

  • A meter can be the scene's main figure. The Statue of Liberty gilds from the base up as coins land, by revealing thirty bands of one gold repaint; the rules say it changes nothing, and it still gives every coin a visible result. It needs one figure painted twice in exact register, not an animation.
  • Gold for what pays, the theme's colours for the stage. Red, white and blue stay in the backdrop, bunting and lettering; coins, medals, ribbons and collectors are gold, so a prize is found at a glance on a busy patriotic screen.
  • A white sticker outline lets detailed, warm, realistic objects read on a pale board. Each pay symbol ships its outline as a separate silhouette sprite.
  • One medal painting, four colours, two sizes covers the jackpot symbols, the jackpot display and the jackpot win screens; a rosette and a starred ribbon are all that mark the top prize.
  • The frame budget went to highlights, not to character animation: 21 of 25 sequences are white sweeps cut to one symbol or prize layer each, 345 of 426 frames. For AI art work this is a repeatable job: one sweep per finished symbol.
  • Build the board in halves. Panel, bunting and flags are drawn once and mirrored, which works because none of them carries lettering.
  • The theme is a dated national occasion (the 250 in the title, the flag, founding figures, Capitol, Liberty Bell), carried by a kit of emblems rather than a story. The same kit of board, medals, collectors and a gilding figure could carry another occasion with new emblems; that this was the studio's intent is inference.
  • From the same provider and framework as Mega Cash Boost: Hold & Win (same file layout, shell, Poppins, skeleton names such as SlotFrame, SceneCollector, TileWild, WinBig), and again every picture is the game's own. Where that game was neon with no scene and no figure, this one is fully painted: the framework fixes the structure and leaves the art direction free.
  • Real historical figures appear as friendly caricatures on symbols. It suits this market and occasion; a studio taking the idea should pick figures and tone deliberately for its own markets.

Art direction Read

StyleFamily-animation cartoon. Pigs and wolf are rounded mascots with big heads and readable expressions; tools (saw, hard hat, tape, toolbox) are chunky and simplified; houses are doll's-house fronts whose material is exaggerated (straw, logs, brick, pale stone). Prize art borrows from fairground and work-site signage.
RenderingSmooth digital painting with airbrushed gradients, strong white gloss highlights, a thin outline of a darker tone and often a pale rim so pieces lift off the dark reel backing. Lettering is fat, bevelled, outlined and rimmed. Effects are flat hand-drawn frames with glow. The background is the one finely textured painting.
ColourWarm cast on a cool stage. Feature and prize art is gold, orange and red (hat and saw rig: #8e2215, #f8ae0c, #d84f07, 88% warm); the background is 84% cool (#143240, #2f7040, #455787, #0d1a88) and the wolf is blue-violet (#56558c). Royals are a single emerald green (#1a6348). Prize tiers keep one colour each wherever they appear: magenta Mini, green Minor, blue Major, red Grand, white-blue Ultra. Measured over the game's own captured art: black #080907 13%, dark blue #162946 7%, orange #f4aa14 7%, dark red #590e23 6%.
LightingNight scene lit from inside the picture by lamps; objects are top-lit with hard gloss. Glow is kept as separate additive layers and outline sprites (hat glow, wedge glow, row highlight), not painted in. On screen the reel window is the darkest area and the wheel and lawn the brightest.
AmbienceCheerful, loud and crowded, as the base-game screens show: the wheel, the rolling sign, six plaques and the logo all compete around a dark reel window, and the calm garden is reduced to a green and blue margin. The wolf is a comic villain, present in the base game only as a tail swishing under the reels. The pace of wins and features is not known from this run.
ShapesRound and chunky everywhere: domed hats, circular saws and coins, rounded topiary, bubble letters. Sharpness is kept for the saw teeth, the wolf's muzzle and ears, and spark bursts.
MaterialsGlossy plastic (hard hats, button), steel, gem-set steel and gold (saws, coins), straw, logs, brick and stone (houses and their frames), fur, clipped hedge and cobbles, varnished wood and brass (the wheel drum), hazard tape, soap bubbles and chrome in the logo.
TypographyDisplay lettering is drawn art: the logo gives each word its own material (wood HUFF, bubble PUFF, chrome GRAND), and prize and feature words are heavy rounded capitals with bevel, outline and rim, coloured by tier. Words are swapped as whole sprites for Spanish (PREMIO for JACKPOT). Running text is Noto Sans as twelve distance-field font pages, with Frutiger Neue in the provider's frame; both are the provider's.
MotionSeen in the real frames: the two wheel rings turn slowly, the 3D sign above rolls from plate to plate, the wolf's tail swishes under the reels (1.33 s animations in the file), and on the one spin the spin button becomes a white stop square. Everything else is read from the files: eleven Spine 4.1.24 skeletons with symbol landings of 1.3 to 3.3 s and wins of 2 to 3 s, the wolf's pop-up (3.1 s in, 6.8 s loop) and blow (1.5 s in, 4.2 s loop), houses that build in 1.2 s and are blown away in 1.0 s, feature banners of 1.8 s, a 1.75 s caution-tape transition and a four-tier big win whose intro grows from 0.4 to 3.1 s. Faces, destruction and wind are drawn frame sequences (up to 89 frames; the three wind sheets total 137). Sprite sheets state 24 frames a second. No skeleton frame is shown in this report: the project's drawing tool does not read Spine 4.1 correctly.
VariantsGrades by recolour on shared rigs: the saw in steel, diamond and gold; the wheel in silver and gold; features in plain, Super and Ultra; four houses on one rig. The hat and mansion blocks in 2x2, 3x3 and 3x5. English and Spanish versions of every worded picture. Landscape and portrait versions of most animations and plaques.
ConstructionPixiJS client. In this run: 140 textures, 1,535 named sprites, 11 skeletons, 3 fonts, 48 frame sequences. Sprite sheets are 'Red 7 Exporter' packs; skeletons are Spine 4.1.24 with few meshes and many additive slots; parts of one rig share one canvas size so grades, houses and banners swap part for part (saw parts 360x374, house parts 360x360, banner parts 1148x720). The background is one square 1920x1920 picture for both orientations. The reel board is a plain see-through dark rectangle with no drawn frame. The sign is a glTF model with a 1024x1024 texture; the wheel is assembled from wedge sprites.
ConsistencyHigh: one outline-and-gloss treatment on every object, one lettering system, one colour per prize tier (blue-white for the top: Ultra, diamond saw, mansion frame), and the building-site motif carried into signs, stripes and the transition. The Buy Pass dialog's buttons are the one generic-looking set. The wolf's howling-moon win picture is a deliberate change of register.

What to take from it Read

  • Keep the bonus in sight: the prize wheel turns permanently behind see-through reels and the sign above rolls through the features, so the top prizes are on screen on every spin. It costs a busy picture; the plain dark reel window is what keeps the symbols readable.
  • Set a warm, glossy cast on a cool, dark stage: the background measures 84% cool, the feature symbols 88% warm.
  • Tell the premium tier apart three ways at once: gold, a glowing patterned backing, and size beyond the cell. The royals are one colour and sit inside the cell.
  • Give each prize tier one colour and use it on every surface that names the tier: coin, plaque title, wheel wedge, halo. Reserve blue-white for the top.
  • Build grades as swaps on a shared rig and a shared canvas size: three saws from one animation set, four houses from one rig, eleven feature banners from one skeleton.
  • Rig what moves mechanically and draw what is chaotic: houses build from rigged parts and are destroyed in drawn frames; the wolf's body is rigged and his face is drawn.
  • Make the celebration from the cast: the big win is the wolf blowing down a better house per tier, and its particles are the game's own coin, hat and saw.
  • Carry the theme into the system art: hazard stripes for Super and Ultra, a road-sign diamond for the wheel, caution tape for the transition.
  • For an AI art package on this model the static pieces are few and large: one square background, about 18 symbol stills at 300 px, four houses with matching frames and backings, a coin with swappable words, wedges and plates with words, a logo. The cost sits in the drawn sequences (destruction, wind, swirls), which is where generated art would need the most hand work.
  • Limits of this report: seen on real screens are the loading screen, the base-game layout, eleven of the eighteen symbols, the turning wheel, the rolling sign, the wolf's tail and one spin. The free-play session expired after that spin, so every win, the hard hat and buzz saw features, the wolf's pop-up and blow, the houses, the wheel feature, free spins, the big win, the transition, the Buy Pass panel and the paytable are read from the files alone (parts, animation names, lengths measured from the skeleton files). No skeleton is drawn here, whatever the method notes below say: the project's drawing tool does not read Spine 4.1 correctly.
