What to take from it Read

  • A new theme on an old frame: every piece here answers a piece of the building-site Huff N' Puff games (saw and hard hat became blue and red balls, toolboxes became goals, houses became trophies, caution tape became team-colour bands), and the files keep the old names. The mechanics, rigs and timings were kept; only the pictures changed. That is the cheapest route to a sequel, and a clear brief for an art package: the list of pieces is already known.
  • Let the theme supply the meters: the two collection pots are goals that fill with balls, and each collected ball visibly travels there on a smoke trail. The player sees progress as an object, not a number.
  • Two team colours do the work of a whole palette: red and blue mark the two feature symbols, the two goals, the fan's face and the transition, on a green field that never competes with them.
  • Keep the bonus in sight: the prize wheel turns permanently behind and above see-through reels, and a wheel symbol visibly upgrades a wedge. The plain dark reel window is what keeps the symbols readable in a crowded screen.
  • Give each prize tier one colour and use it on every surface that names it: plaque title, plaque rim, wheel wedge.
  • Rig what moves mechanically and draw what is chaotic: goals, trophies, coins and panels are rigged from parts; the wolf's faces, the logo's letters and all smoke, wind and sparkle are drawn frames. The drawn sequences are where the texture budget goes (22 pages for one dust blast, 11 for the logo).
  • Make the celebration from the cast: the big win stages the wolf and the three trophies, and its particles are the game's coin, star, boot and ball.
  • Small wins are quiet: ten times the bet got a gold burst and a caption. The spectacle is saved for features and tiers.
  • For an AI art package on this model the static pieces are few: two square backgrounds (one a relight of the other), 16 symbol stills at about 300 px, one trophy in three metals with frames and backings, two goals, a coin, 16 wedges, a logo. The cost sits in the drawn sequences, which is where generated art would need the most hand work.
  • Limits of this report: no feature, free spin, big win, wolf pop-up, transition or later paytable page was reached, so those are read from the files alone. The demo is the UK build; that its art matches the US game is inference. No skeleton is drawn here, whatever the method notes below say: the project's drawing tool does not read Spine 4.1 correctly.

The reel board is a see-through dark panel in a hairline frame. Atlas pages are 2048x2048; the three wolf rigs take 132 of them and the prize meters 54.
ConsistencyHigh: one outline-and-gloss treatment on every object, one lettering system, one colour per prize tier, and the building-site motif carried into symbols, signs, the transition, the feature props and the logo. Two things stand apart: the wolf and the big-win pigs are animated as whole frames while everything else is parts and overlays, and one stray sequence (a fire dragon) belongs to another game. Part names left from the earlier Huff N' Puff games (buzzsaw, wheel) show the rigs were carried over and re-dressed (inference).

What to take from it Read

  • Make the scene the prize board. The mansion is at once background, theme and the place where the feature's prizes sit, colour-banded gold, blue and dark for the three prize ranges; the player reads the top prizes off the house before a spin. A see-through reel panel in a hairline frame is what makes that possible.
  • Carry one motif through every layer. The building site is in the symbols (hat, cones, toolbox), the signs (hazard stripes), the transition (caution tape), the feature props (brush, hammer), the tiers (straw, stick, brick frames) and the logo. Each new feature got one prop and one stripe colour rather than a new look.
  • Sell the features on the loading screen with three cards: the jackpots, the trigger (six hats) and the choice of features. Each is one picture and one line.
  • One colour per prize tier, used on plaques, labels and effects, and one glow colour per house tier (magenta straw, cyan stick, yellow brick). It lets small frames on a busy board be read at a glance.
  • Spend drawn animation where the character is. The wolf's face and the big-win pigs are full-frame sequences; frames, plates, coins and signs are stills moved by a rig with glow overlays. For our AI art work this splits the job cleanly: stills and overlays suit generation and re-tinting, the acted sequences need an animator or a consistent frame-by-frame method.
  • Tiers by re-dressing a rig: straw, stick and brick share bones and canvas sizes, and the same three house paintings serve as reel symbols, paytable pictures, feature houses and big-win props.
  • Repainting beats tinting for time of day: the night mansion has its own lit windows and lantern light, and the prize plates have day and night versions to match.
  • What it costs: three near-identical wolf rigs on 132 atlas pages, two near-identical symbol rigs and a stray sequence from another game. A build audit would have saved a large share of the download; worth a check on our own builds.
  • Not seen in play, so not yet a reference for us: the wolf himself, the free spins, the four features, jackpot awards, the big win and the paytable's lower pages. In about 32 base spins no feature came and this demo shows no Buy Pass button; a longer played session is still needed before using this game as a motion or pacing reference.

A fruit-and-letters slot rebuilt as a neon scoreboard: no scene and no character, only red laser light, a thin neon reel frame, and fifteen glowing prize plates that lightning keeps charging while three colours of diamond wait to collect them.

Palette Measured

  • #fafaf8 light yellow 21.0%
  • #f7c030 orange 11.6%
  • #f08617 orange 10.6%
  • #f2292e red 10.0%
  • #d1c9ce grey 4.3%
  • #ab2b0f red 3.7%
  • #f8656e red 3.3%
  • #19083b dark purple 2.5%

ComponentUnits

Art direction Read

StyleFlat neon graphic design around glossy 3D-look symbols. The backdrop, the frame and the prize plates are pure light and outline; the fruit, bolts and wild button are airbrushed casino illustration; the diamonds are low-polygon gems. Everything leans: letters, plates and beams share one forward slant.
RenderingTwo kinds only. Light: white shapes with feathered edges, tinted and added by the game (backdrop soft edge 0.713, lightning 0.738, glows 0.951). Objects: smooth volumes or flat facets with hard outer edges and a thin blue rim (fruit 0.075, diamonds 0.042, boost 0.1). Lettering has a two-band chrome face with a hard horizon line and a stepped extruded side.
ColourRed field, gold and cyan signs. Measured over the art files: near-white #fafaf8 21% (the white light sprites, which the game tints), gold #f7c030 11%, orange #f08617 10%, red #f2292e 10%, dark red #ab2b0f 3%, dark purple-blue #19083b 2%. On screen the backdrop is set by tints in the skeleton files: near-black wine #1f0014 under red #be1000 and #ff0000 beams. The code is strict: cyan-blue is Cash (plates, Blue Diamond, blue Booster), gold is Jackpot (plates, Gold Diamond, gold Booster), red is both (Red Diamond, the frame, the field), and the logo's three words carry the same three colours. Purple belongs to the Wild alone.
LightingSelf-lit neon everywhere; there is no light source in a scene because there is no scene. Objects are lit from the top or top-left with a blue rim from below, as if standing on a lit sign. Glow circles behind the board make the centre the brightest area.
AmbienceHigh voltage, arcade and motorsport: fast, loud, synthetic. The mood comes from motion of light, not from a place or a story.
ShapesThe slanted parallelogram (plates, backplates, frame corners), the chevron (board pattern, meter fill, boost arrows), the lightning zigzag (logo, letters' notches, the container's ends, the effects) and the faceted diamond. Circles appear only on the Wild and the coin.
MaterialsNeon tube, dark glass, coloured chrome lettering, moulded glossy plastic or glass (bolts, wild button), fruit skin and flesh, cut crystal, polished gold coin, electricity.
TypographyHeavy slanted capitals throughout, in two related faces: a wide italic sans with chrome bands for the logo, WILD and BOOST, and the condensed Anton for numbers, jackpot names, win tiers and captions (gold two-band numerals with a red-brown side; a white set for small counts). The low symbols 10 to A are lettering too, cut by a bolt. Small interface text is the provider shell's Poppins (Regular, SemiBold, Bold).
MotionAll motion is Spine 4.2.43: 54 skeletons in one bundle file, moving, scaling and tinting still pictures, plus 14 hand-drawn frame sequences (278 frames), of which eight are lightning (150 frames), three are the diamonds' turn (75), and the rest a coin, a win-line bolt and a plate border. Seen in play: the red beams sweeping behind the board all the time; an opening sequence in which two large Boosters and then a large red diamond appear over the reels and charge the plates; a Booster on the reels growing to cover the board when it fires; plate values jumping with a flash; white-blue lightning crackling along the frame and around locked diamonds; coins flying from a diamond up to a plate; a lightning bolt along a paying line with the amount in gold numerals; in the bonus a yellow flash that turns the stage gold, diamonds blurring through single cells, bolts carrying prizes from the plates to the diamonds, and BIG WIN with a coin shower. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7.
VariantsTwo states of the whole stage from one set of parts (normal and special skins: red for the base game, orange-gold with yellow beams for the Hold & Win, both seen in play); two states of every plate outline (resting and red); cash and jackpot plates as one component in two colours; three diamonds and two Boosters as recolours of one design each; desktop and mobile plate shapes; a brighter Add copy of almost every symbol for win flashes.
ConstructionThree 4096 px atlas pages hold 391 sprites, more than half of them animation frames; there is no background picture at all (the backdrop is a 202 px white square and a glow circle, stretched and tinted). Symbols are layered: fruit in two halves, wild as button and word, Booster and Diamond as plate, object and word or bolt. Five localised lettering files (en-GB). The paytable pictures, logo copy, numeral fonts and interface come from the provider's shared services.
ConsistencyVery high: one slant, three shapes and three prize colours run through backdrop, frame, plates, symbols, lettering and effects. The only seam is between the softly painted fruit and the hard graphic world around it, and the blue rim on the fruit is there to close it.

What to take from it Read

  • A slot can ship with no background painting and no character: tinted white shapes moved by a rig gave this game its whole stage in eleven sprites, and a second stage for the bonus by changing tint values. For AI art work this moves the effort from illustration to a small kit of clean light shapes.
  • Make the prizes the picture. Fifteen neon plates take more of the screen than the reels' frame, and every Booster visibly changes a number on them; the art direction serves a mechanic of growing prizes rather than a theme.
  • One colour code end to end: blue is Cash, gold is Jackpot, red is both, on plates, diamonds, Boosters, backplates and even the three words of the logo. A player learns the rules from the colours.
  • Spend drawn frames on one effect family and reuse it: 150 of 278 animation frames are white lightning, tinted cyan or gold and placed by rigs on the frame, the plates, the logo and the symbols.
  • Classic fruit made current by cutting, not repainting: each fruit is two small pictures, a cut half and a whole half, which gives depth and a win animation; the letters get the theme from a single bolt-shaped notch.
  • Reserve one hand-animated asset for the symbol players stare at: the three diamonds each have a 25-frame turn, while every other symbol moves by rig only.
  • From the same provider as Fire Rail Express: Hold & Win, and built on the same framework (same file layout, 20 skeleton names in common, the same shell, Poppins and Double Chance card, byte-identical glow, line and lineEnd helpers), yet no picture of the game's own art is shared: same-named sprites such as coin_00 or win1Txt are different drawings. The reuse is in structure and tooling, not in art.
  • A numeral style picked from a provider font library (gold Anton here, purple-and-gold in Fire Rail Express) is enough to tie changing numbers to the game's lettering without drawing digits per game.

Art direction Read

StyleTwo manners side by side. Symbols, pots, gong and firecrackers are glossy, toy-like stylised objects. The emperor is a realistic painted figure. The setting is not a place but ornament: a red ground pressed with a wave-scale pattern, cloud scrolls and Greek-key bands. The interface buttons are a neutral charcoal set outside the theme.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed gradients with hard silhouettes, a gold or light rim and white star glints on every object; lettering with a white outline and a dark extrusion; effects as soft light on black. Nothing has a drawn black outline. Measured hard-edged overall (soft edge 0.07).
ColourRed and gold with almost no cool colour: measured over the game's own art, dark red #600d04 at 20% and near-black #1d0d08 at 18% lead, then gold-orange #edb517 at 8%; warm 74% against cool 4%, saturation 0.62, brightness 0.39. Hues are orange 43%, red 33%, yellow 19%, green 3%. Colour outside red and gold is rationed and always means something: green #06ed61 is the money ball, green, blue, purple and red-gold are the gong's four features, and each jackpot tier has a colour of its own (Grand red, Major green, Maxi purple, Minor blue, Mini orange); magenta is the top prize's figure; the multiplier is red with a white outline.
LightingOne top light on everything (measured from the top on 174 parts, top-right on 32, top-left on 19) with specular glints on the gold; the backgrounds are dark with a low glow, so the gold objects are the light of the screen. The base reel backing is the darkest surface (#550202, brightness 0.07).
AmbienceFestive, lucky and rich: New Year firecrackers, coins, pots of gold and a laughing emperor. Calm in the base game, where the screen is a dark red wall with gold furniture; the bonus spins turn the board itself gold.
ShapesCircles everywhere: gong, coins, money balls, jackpot discs, round buttons, the ring in the background, the bonus wheel. Around them, cloud scrolls and a Greek-key band as the two ornaments, and pill-shaped plaques for every figure. The lettering is the one angular element.
MaterialsPolished gold above all; red lacquer and enamel; glass or jade balls; brocade and gold metalwork on the emperor; paper firecrackers; smoked glass for the buttons.
TypographyThe logo is heavy angular faux-brush capitals in bevelled yellow gold with a deep red extrusion. Jackpot names and MONEY GONG BONUS are drawn in the same faux-brush manner; two such faces are embedded (Gang of Three and Nuku Nuku), which is probably where they come from (inference). The three feature words are rounded poster capitals, one colour each. Running text is live Noto Sans (Black, Condensed Black, Condensed Bold, Regular) with Passion One. Figures are bitmap sets drawn per place: white for the bonus spins, magenta and gold for ball values, brown-lacquer and yellow for the Money Gong Bonus.
MotionSpine skeletons carry all of it: 16 skeletons in Spine 4.0 or 4.1 (the report header counts 30 files because 14 layout files of the client are counted with them). By their animation names: every symbol has a win, the money ball four landings, the gong turns like a coin to a feature face and is struck, pots grow and are hit by coins, firecrackers are lit and go off, four win tiers come in, loop and leave, and the emperor pops up with a scroll. Around them, 42 frame sequences (494 frames) of sparks, sweeps, trails and bursts, and nine particle files. No skeleton frame is shown: the project's drawing tool is written for Spine 3.7 and drew none of these; the six real screens show only the base game, the intro and a spin, so movement is read from names and parts and is inference throughout.
VariantsOne base ground, one curtain scene for the intro, and a board that changes backing from dark red to gold for the bonus spins; a Hold & Win grid and a round Money Gong Bonus wheel as feature scenes (parts only, not seen in play). Every reel symbol ships sharp and motion-blurred. The money ball comes green and gold, plain and with four jackpot names. The gong has five faces. Landscape only was captured; portrait animations are named in the files.
Construction1,127 named sprites on 54 textures in 51 units, 49 of them the game's own art. Solid art is PNG in TexturePacker sheets or Spine atlases; effects are JPEG on black on separate pages of the same atlas; backgrounds are single JPEGs with no layers (1584x720, the curtain 3168x1440). A reel symbol is about 300x270 for a cell of about 313x302; the emperor of the pop-up is the largest art (head 899x801). Half of the reel frame is shipped and mirrored (inference). Three skeletons (the two ambients and the transition) ship only a placeholder.
ConsistencyVery tight. One emblem at four sizes, two ornaments, one top light and a two-colour palette hold every screen together, and the few other colours are a code the player learns on the intro panel and meets again on the gong, the balls and the meters. The loose ends are the neutral grey buttons and the plain sans win titles, which belong to the provider's kit more than to the game.

What to take from it Read

  • A feature can be the art direction. The gong is a symbol, the title's coin, the trigger device and the bonus wheel's centre: one well-made emblem reused at four sizes does the work of several separate illustrations.
  • Colour is used as a code, not as decoration. On an almost entirely red and gold screen, green means money ball, four colours mean the four features and each jackpot tier has its own, taught once on the intro panel and repeated on gong, balls and meters.
  • No scenery at all. The background is a patterned wall with a seat for the gong; the board changes from dark red to gold for the bonus spins. A leading game here spends nothing on a landscape.
  • Royals are cheap and still on theme: five letters in one red brush stroke with a gold edge, no ornament each, readable on a near-black reel backing.
  • The only painted character is saved for the top symbol and the pop-up host, cut into a few large parts. Everything else that moves is an object.
  • Effects are greyscale or gold light on black, shipped apart from the solid art and shaped to their object (a light sweep per wordmark, a glow per silhouette). That split is a production pattern an AI art pipeline can follow: generate solid pieces, derive masks and glows from their outlines.
  • Pre-rendered blur: every reel symbol has a second, motion-blurred picture. Plan two outputs per symbol.
  • Several drawn number sets, each tied to one place and prize, instead of one font: figures are treated as art.

Art direction Read

StylePainterly realism for the scene and the picture symbols (market goods drawn as still lifes), rendered 3D for everything that moves in space (the genie, lamps, coins, gems, tiles), and ornamental gold scrollwork on deep red for the frame and plaques. The lettering is a family of its own: storybook display scripts with 3D extrusion.
RenderingNo outlines anywhere. Objects are softly lit and detailed; each picture symbol sits in a halo of coloured smoke instead of a tile. Gold is thin, crisp and bright; glass buttons and lamps have a hard top highlight. Effects are photographic smoke, fire and lightning added over the art.
ColourMeasured over the game's own art, the palette is led by near-black #0a0509 (26%), dark red #501614 (8%) and dark blue-violet #2c2842 (8%), then near-white #f7f8f5 and golds #f6d117 and #f9f15c. On screen the board is deep red with gold, the street warm orange and rose with violet-blue shadow, and the controls violet and blue with yellow glyphs. Colour carries meaning: each picture symbol has one smoke colour (violet, yellow, orange-red, green), each lamp one glass colour (blue Collect, pearl Jackpot, orange Ignite), each of the five prizes one title colour (red Grand, green Major, magenta Maxi, cyan Minor, orange Mini), and magenta-pink is kept for money won (the win frame and the win digits). The bonus cave turns the whole palette cool: blue #474ebe leads it at 56%.
LightingTwo lights in the base scene: warm lantern light from the stalls and the ground, cool dusk from above. Symbols are lit softly from the upper left with their smoke as a back light. Lamps glow from inside. The cave is lit by blue shafts from above.
AmbienceA warm, rich evening market with a secret in it; friendly rather than mysterious, because the genie smiles and the smoke is pink. The cave is the cold, magical counter-scene.
ShapesRound and generous: bottle-bellied lamps, dome buttons, coins, cushion and heart-shaped gems, fat rounded royals. The frame answers with thin straight rails ending in curls. Smoke puffs and spirals soften every edge.
MaterialsPolished and chased gold, red velvet or damask, blown glass, cut gemstones, brass, fruit, olive oil, woven carpet, stone and wood in the street, smoke, fire and lightning.
TypographyFour lettering families, all gold-based. The wordmarks: Mystery of the Lamp in a gold storybook serif with swashes, Secret Bazaar in red and gold slab capitals. The lamp words (Collect, Jackpot, Ignite) in a yellow decorative script with coloured 3D sides. The prize titles in a round seventies-style script, one colour each. Numerals in a tall fat Didone-like serif as bitmap fonts: gold chrome with a coloured edge for each prize, pink chrome for wins, ivory, yellow and orange for coin values. Big-win words are plain fat sans capitals in gold on a deep layered extrusion. Labels (TOTAL BET, WIN, BALANCE) are live text in Oswald; Yeseva One is embedded too.
MotionSpine 4.0 skeletons throughout (18 binary skeleton files, each with an opaque and an alpha page), mixing rigged parts with short frame sequences. The tools here read only JSON skeletons of older versions, so none was drawn, and the 10 skeletons counted at the top of this report are JSON files of a promotional overlay loaded by the demo host (prize tickets, chests, cards), not this game's. What follows is from the frame sequences, the names in the files and the real screens. Reels use pre-blurred copies of every symbol. Gems land wrapped in white lightning and send small gems up to their lamp, whose gold pile grows in three steps. The wild is a rolled carpet that unrolls over 39 frames to show WILD or 2X. Wins darken the board, put a magenta neon frame with a running light on each winning cell and count the amount in pink digits. The genie is a rig with IK that sways over a billowing smoke column, her hands glowing. Smoke (two puffs, many tints) loops behind the logo, the lamp words and the prize plaques. The big-win words are built letter by letter in five tiers; a coin stream and a spinning lamp are the transitions (inference from their skeletons; not reached in play).
VariantsTwo scenes (bazaar, cave), each in landscape and portrait. Every symbol as a still and a blurred copy; picture symbols also as object and halo apart. One lamp design in three colours, one treasure pile in three sizes for each. One prize plaque in five titles, one numeral face in nine colourings. One button design in four states for every function. One bonus tile in blue and gold.
Construction987 named sprites on 54 atlas pages (1,011 components and 77 textures with the fonts, loose pictures and the demo host's overlay), 43 frame sequences holding 664 frames, 4 embedded fonts of the game. The client served its sheets from a folder named mobile: symbol cells are 164x145 and buttons 200x200, close to what a 1280x720 screen shows, while backgrounds are 2040x1410. Whether a larger pack exists for other devices is not known from this capture. Art is split by blend, not by subject: each skeleton has a page of opaque plates for additive light and a page with alpha. Greyscale and white effect art is tinted in the engine. Much is pre-rendered from 3D (gem turns, tile tumbles, word swings, coin flips) rather than rigged.
ConsistencyHigh. One palette rule (red and gold board, violet controls, magenta for wins), one material set and one binding motif, smoke, run from the loading picture to the smallest effect. The lettering is the loosest part: five display faces share only their gold. Two file names for symbols do not match their pictures, a trace of an earlier symbol set (inference).

What to take from it Read

  • Smoke is the system: two white puffs and a spiral, tinted and looped, give the logo, the lamps, the prizes, the symbols' halos and the transitions one common atmosphere at almost no texture cost.
  • Picture symbols need no tile. A soft halo in the symbol's own colour separates it from the board and codes it at a glance; the royals are kept in one red so they recede.
  • Colour is assigned once and reused: one hue per lamp feature, per prize tier and per symbol, and one hue (magenta-pink) reserved for money won. A player can read the state of the game from colour alone.
  • The feature is always on screen: three lamps with growing gold piles sit on the reel frame from the first spin, so the promise of the bonus is part of the base composition, not a separate meter.
  • Split art by blend mode: an opaque page of light effects on black and an alpha page per animation. It keeps files small and is a pattern worth copying in our own pipeline.
  • Pre-rendered 3D in short sequences (11 to 39 frames) does the work of complex rigs for gems, coins, tiles and word turns; only the genie has a real character rig, and even she fakes her turn from rendered views (inference).
  • Build win words from letters with separate extruded backs: five tier titles fit on one small page and can animate letter by letter.
  • For AI-assisted art: the still-life symbols and the two matte-painting scenes are the kind of picture an image model makes well; the value this game adds is in the strict colour coding, the gold ornament drawn clean, and the motion design, which still need an artist's system.

A lost-temple jungle in which every game mechanic is a snake: a photoreal misty rainforest sits behind hard, glossy, gold-rimmed symbols, three jewel-scaled Snakes in red, green and blue run the features, and a stone serpent above the reels heats from grey to lava as coins are thrown into its mouth.

Art direction Read

StyleTwo registers kept apart on purpose. The world (two jungle scenes, branches, birds) is photoreal painted concept art with soft haze; the game pieces (letters, props, coin, Snakes, plates, frame) are stylised casino art with thick gold rims, enamel colour and Mesoamerican step-fret ornament. The stone serpent and the temple walls sit between the two. Inference: the backgrounds have the look of an image model's picture retouched by hand; the symbols and interface are drawn in the usual production way.
RenderingBackgrounds: soft atmospheric depth, no outlines. Symbols: smooth gradients, hard speculars, a dark outline and a thin yellow-green edge glow that lifts them off the dark panel. Snakes: faceted glossy scales and gold trim. Lettering: two-tone gradient fills with a light inner edge and dark outline. Effects: white sprites tinted by the engine, with fire and lava painted in colour.
ColourMeasured over the game's art: near-black brown #18130f 29%, jungle grey-green #526254 14%, dark wine #392d2c 10%, pale grey #b8b7b5 6%, orange-brown #a53b11 5%, near-white #f9f9f7 4%, pale green #83927f 3%, deep red #601a0a 1%. The base game is green haze around a dark brown board with gold; the bonus turns the surround to red stone, violet and orange. Colour carries the rules: red, green and blue for Collect, Clone and Double (heads, frames, gems, side lights, the NEW SNAKE words); purple, blue, green, red-orange and gold for MINI, MINOR, MAJOR, GRAND and ULTIMATE; one hue per letter symbol; gold for anything that pays; jade green for the value on a coin.
LightingDiffuse daylight from above through mist in the base scene; a low orange sun and coloured haze in the bonus. Game pieces are lit from the top with their own highlights and do not take the scene's light. The statue is lit from above until its mouth and eyes light it from inside.
AmbienceAn expedition that has found the temple: humid, hushed and green at first, with danger shown as beauty (jewel snakes, a sleeping statue). The bonus is heat and treasure: red walls, gold underfoot, the statue's eyes burning.
ShapesDiamond snake heads and shield-shaped hoods; trapezoid plates in stepped-fret frames; slanted slab letters; round sun coins with spikes; square spiral frets on every frame end, lock plate and letter serif. The fret and the snake are the two repeated marks: the Wild, the win line's end, the win plate's ornament, the frame's corner and the opening wipe are all snakes.
MaterialsWet leaf, moss and mist; carved stone, grey when cold and red when lit; gold with turquoise; enamel or gemstone scales; coloured glass letters; lava and ember.
TypographyDrawn words in slanted comic capitals with a dark outline for jackpots, win tiers and feature messages, each in its tier's or snake's colour. The logo is separate: spaced serif capitals in snake skin, gold and red. Numbers come from three bitmap fonts of the provider's shared store: Rubik Mono One in gold with a deep wine extrusion (ladder multipliers, win amounts), Blambot FX Pro Heavy in jade with a gold rim (the value on a Golden Coin, as the screens show), Anton italic in gold (the collector counters). The shell's Poppins sets the help, buttons and balance line.
MotionAll motion is Spine: 57 skeletons in one bundle file (47 in 4.2.40, 6 in 4.2.42, 4 in 4.2.43), with 29 frame sequences (515 frames: the coin's turn, a lava flow, fire, white glints fitted to each letter, word and plate, sparks, mist, two shatters). Seen in play: snake bodies wiping the intro away; the three collector frames arriving and the red Snake unlocking under a blue sparkling splash; coins flying from each Golden Coin to the statue, whose mouth and eyes turn red; clusters bound in a gold chain with a 3-2-1 lock disc; win lines in gold with a snake-head end; a gold win amount with a coin shower; the temple walls sliding in for the bonus. Read from the files only: jackpot wins, the big-win tiers, the Clone and Double Snakes in action. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer cannot draw Spine 4; assembled and motion pictures are absent for that reason only.
VariantsTwo scenes on one picture (day, and a dusk regrade). Three Snakes on one rig with identical part sizes. Five jackpot plates on one shape, drawn twice (ladder size and win size). Three win tiers and a total on one lettering. Three collector frames told apart by gems and side lights. Two reel backings (five and six reels) and a frame cut in strips so the board grows from 5x4 to 6x6. Numerals in three coloured fonts.
ConstructionThree 4096 px atlas pages hold the game: two carry one 2750x2510 scene each with the large pieces, the third some 600 small sprites. Eleven word pictures are localised (en-GB). Characters are few and cheap: the statue is one still with glow layers, a Snake is seven parts, the screen-filling wipe is six 307 px scale strips run along a path. Water moves by a displacement map over a mask, not by frames. White effect sprites are tinted in the engine. Symbol pictures for the help, the flat logo, the numeral fonts, the Extra Chance card, the controls and Poppins come from the provider's shared store outside the game bundle. The artists' green cell guide (tileGuide) ships in the atlas as an anchor.
ConsistencyStrong inside each register, with one visible seam between them: the soft photoreal jungle and the hard enamel game pieces do not share light or edge quality, and the birds, painted sharper than the scene, sit between. The seam is used rather than hidden: the dark board and gold rims make every symbol read at once against the haze. Colour coding is exact across symbol, frame, word and effect. The comic-capital win words are the least themed element.

What to take from it Read

  • Let one creature carry every mechanic. Here the snake is the Wild, the three feature symbols, the collectors, the progress statue, the payline's end, the win plate's ornament and the screen wipe, so the theme is restated by play itself and needs no mascot character.
  • Give each feature a colour and never break it: red Collect, green Clone, blue Double hold across head, frame gems, side lights, splash words and effects. A player can read which feature fired from colour alone, and one rig with three skins serves all three.
  • Show locked content as dimmed real art, not as a padlock. The Clone and Double Snakes sit dark in their frames with a counter from the first spin: the goal is visible and the same sprites are reused.
  • Put a progress display where the eye already rests and make it a material change. The stone serpent goes from cold grey to lava mouth and burning eyes with a handful of glow layers and one 40-frame lava loop over a single still picture.
  • A photoreal background can sit behind stylised symbols if the board between them is dark and plain and every symbol has a rim. Decide that separation on purpose; do not try to half-match the two.
  • Make the bonus by regrading and re-dressing, not repainting: the same jungle picture in dusk colours, two temple wall pieces and a coin pile sliding in, and a second reel backing give a scene that feels new.
  • Build big moments from small tiles. The opening wipe fills the screen with snake bodies made of six scale strips on a path; the cluster chain is five 68 px pieces. Plan such pieces as tileable from the start.
  • Fit the highlight to the object. Each letter, word and plate has its own short white glint sequence drawn to its bevels, at small size and scaled up: cheap, and far better than a generic sweep.
  • Keep effect sprites white and tint them in the engine, and keep painted colour for the few effects that are material (fire, lava).
  • For AI-assisted art: backgrounds of this kind are where an image model gives most (two scenes from one picture by regrade); symbols, frames, plates and lettering here depend on exact shape language, rigs in parts and colour codes, and are the part to art-direct tightly and cut for animation.

Art direction Read

StyleStorybook cartoon in two registers: painted animation-background landscapes and feature-film style characters (the wolf, three pigs), against inflated glossy letters and toy tools with a pig's snout worked into each. Interface plates are the materials themselves, a straw bale, a plank, a brick panel.
RenderingBackgrounds and props are painterly with visible brushwork; characters are smoothly blended with sharp speculars and a light rim; letters, tools, logo and numerals are flat gradients with gloss bands and thick dark outlines. Effects are flat white hand-drawn smoke, dust and wind, with soft white glows added on top.
ColourMeasured over the game's art: dark forest greens #192f29 19% and #375d56 10%, near-white #eef2f0 9% (smoke, numerals), brick brown #8d3d17 6%, warm yellow #f3d07a 6%, sky blues #6498bd 6% and #a7cfe1 4%, straw #efdaae 2%. The scene is green and blue, the interface warm brown, tan and gold, and the symbols take one saturated hue each. Jackpots are coded by colour: MINI magenta, MINOR blue, MAJOR green, MEGA red-orange, GRAND gold. Frame metal ranks the pigs: steel, copper, gold.
LightingDaylight from the upper right in the base scene and a low sunset behind the hills in the special scene; props and plates are lit from the upper left; characters have a warm key and a thin cool rim. Nothing glows by itself except a plate being boosted.
AmbienceSunny, rustic and good-humoured. The base game is a building site in a meadow at midday; the intro shows the finished village at sunset with the wolf waiting. Threat is played as comedy.
ShapesRound and soft everywhere: balloon letters, fat tools, plump pigs, puffed clouds and bushes. The pig's snout (an oval with two dots) is the repeated mark, on every letter, the tape measure, the hard hat, the toolbox, the coin and the reel panel's watermark. Square frames are kept for the Wilds and houses only.
MaterialsStraw, rough timber, fired brick, glossy enamel and plastic, gold coin, denim, fur, skin; flat white smoke and dust.
TypographyTwo voices. Drawn balloon capitals with uneven baselines for the logo, the jackpot names and the win tiers, each word in its own colour; a fat rounded numeral face from the provider's shared font store in white (MarvinRound, on the ladders) and gold (MarvinRoundYellow, for jackpots and wins). HOLD & WIN and its rule line use the rounded face. The help, buttons and balance line are the shell's Poppins.
MotionAll motion is Spine: 41 skeletons in one bundle file (38 in 4.2.43; BonusSpinsSplash, ForegroundEffects and Foregrounds in 4.1.24) moving still pictures and cut-up characters, with 20 hand-drawn frame sequences (283 frames: the piggy coin's turn, plate bursts and sweeps in three materials, dust, wind, the wolf's breath, air rings and swirls on the tools, a frame glint, butterflies). Seen in play: the logo's words dropping in, the Boost sign growing across bleached reels and its word flying to a plate that flares and rises, a reel flashing pink under a landing Wild, winning symbols growing with a gold line, an air ring round the tape measure, a BIG WIN presented by the Straw Farmer pig. Not seen: the bonus, in which by the files the wolf inhales and blows (3.23 s) and the houses burst open. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer cannot draw Spine 4; assembled and motion pictures are absent for that reason only.
VariantsTwo scenes on one composition (day building site, sunset village). Three pigs on one portrait layout and, by their parts, one rig. Three houses, each whole and destroyed. Three prize plates and three plate effects on one timing. Five jackpot names and five sets of coloured brick strips. Three win tiers and a total on one lettering. One numeral face in two colourings.
ConstructionTwo 4096 px atlas pages hold 453 sprites, each page carrying one 2750 px scene; four lettering files are localised (en-GB). Characters and houses are cut into parts for Spine (the wolf 43 sprites with breath, the pigs 32, the houses 33). The reel backing and its pig watermark are grey and tinted by the engine. The flat symbol pictures, the flat logo, the numeral fonts, the Extra Chance card, the controls and Poppins come from the provider's shared store, outside the game bundle.
ConsistencyVery consistent: one idea (three materials in rising strength) orders the Wilds, houses, ladders, win tiers and effects, and one mark (the snout) themes every filler symbol. The joins that show are between the painted characters and the flat glossy letters, which are two different finishes on the same reel, and the plain gold reel frame, which belongs to neither. Shared with the other Octoplay runs (Fire Rail Express, 777 Hot Reels): the shell, Poppins, the Extra Chance card `buyChances2x` (the same file) and three light sprites (circularWhiteRays2, glowSquare, whiteGlow, pixel for pixel); 22 and 24 of the 41 skeleton names also appear in those runs, one scene template (inference). A sprite reading BOILERPLATE is left in the atlas.

What to take from it Read

  • Pick one ordering idea from the theme and use it for everything that has ranks. Here straw, wood and brick rank the Wilds (x1, x2, x3), the houses, the prize ladders and the win tiers, so the player learns the scale once.
  • Theme the filler symbols with one small mark instead of new drawings: a snout on each letter and tool was enough to make 10 to A belong to the tale.
  • Make interface plates out of the theme's materials. The prize cells are a bale, a plank and a brick panel, each one sprite repeated five times, and they give the screen its character more than the reel frame does.
  • Hold the best character back. The wolf is the largest drawing in the game (740x1374 px body, three heads) and appears only on the intro and in the bonus.
  • Let a character present the win: the BIG WIN reuses the Wild pig's bust and the scene's props (hay bale, board, daisies) rather than a separate celebration set.
  • One effect language keeps a cartoon coherent: every effect here is flat white smoke, dust or wind, drawn by hand in 5 to 27 frames, with generic soft glows for light.
  • For AI art work: the scenes are two paintings on one composition (same path, same framing trees, different hour and state), a clear brief for a day and sunset pair; the three pigs are one portrait layout with costume, prop and frame metal changed, a clear brief for consistent character variants.
  • Cut characters and breakable props into parts from the start: each house exists whole and destroyed in loose pieces so one skeleton can stage the collapse on any cell.
  • Grey art tinted in the engine (the reel backing and watermark) is a cheap way to recolour a board per mode.
  • Draw words separately from what they label and keep them in localised files; the logo's four words and the BOOST word are separate sprites so they can animate and travel.

A licensed film adventure staged as a lantern-lit pirate cave: realistic painted portraits of the film's characters and a skeleton pirate host set among cartoon-bold gold lettering and jewel-bright treasure, almost entirely warm orange and gold against one navy reel board, with cyan and acid green kept as signal colours.

Art direction Read

StyleTwo registers side by side. Likeness art (four portrait symbols and one full-length figure) is semi-realistic film-poster painting. Everything else is stylised painted cartoon realism: props such as chests, coins, a ship's wheel, scrolls and chains painted with full materials, and a faceted, animation-background cave. One-Eyed Willy, a skull in a green tricorn hat with a gold eye patch, is the mascot and appears as symbol, map icon, intro host and transition mark.
RenderingFully painted, no line outlines on objects; heavy dark outlines only on lettering. Props carry real material detail (wood grain, rust, hammered metal) at small sizes with hard top-left highlights. The cave is flat faceted planes with soft gradients only in light. Light effects are separate soft additive pictures (the files sit on black or are plain glows), so glow is a layer, not paint.
ColourMeasured over the game's own art: black-brown #1c0c0c 19%, brown #572817 18% and #8e4b23 15%, then light gold #f8eb87 3% and one dark blue #273145 2%. Almost every unit measures 80 to 100% warm. The reel board is the exception (dark blue #152035, 94% of its unit) and is what the gold symbols are read against. Identity colours are used as codes, not decoration: blue, red and green for the three chests and their bonus symbols; gold, green, red and blue for the four collectors; yellow, green, blue and red for the four jackpot plates; cyan (#0cceff) for anticipation and One-Eyed Willy Spins; acid green (#53ff60, #78ff0b) for the Mystery Symbol and the lock.
LightingThe scene has three lights by colour: orange from the skull-shaped cave mouth and two lanterns, teal-green daylight behind the stair, purple in the shadowed rock, with a warm pool on the floor under the reels. Objects are lit from the top left. Prizes glow from inside (coin heaps, the ruby, the chests), and every win or feature state is an added coloured light in the object's own shape.
AmbienceAdventure, not horror: a treasure hunt by lantern light, with skeletons played for fun and the film's catchphrases (NEVER SAY DIE!, HEY YOU GUYS!) used as art. The board always shows the long game: the trail map above and the three chests beside the reels.
ShapesChunky and irregular: hand-cut slab letters, torn parchment, hammered coins with uneven rims, faceted rock. The reel cell is a wide 215x180 rectangle, 6 reels by 4 rows; the collector grows from one cell to a 215x720 column. Round medallions and rectangles with value plates repeat across the prize symbols.
MaterialsParchment and turned wood with brass caps (scrolls, map), dark ship planks (board, panels), gold in three finishes (hammered doubloon, stamped skull coin, plain cartoon disc), ruby and cut gems, rusted iron (chains, the Treasure Wheel), bone, cobweb, lantern glass.
TypographyFour lettering families, all as pictures or bitmap fonts (nine font pages with BMFont .xml files; the only embedded web font is the shell's Roboto Black). A curly storybook pirate serif for values and counters; fat comic block capitals with gradient, extrusion and dark outline for feature names, each in its identity colour; angular faceted slab numerals in gold for win amounts and in silver for free-spin counts; and wide serif capitals that look cut from rusted copper for the big-win tiers. The logo is the film's own lettering.
Motion68 Spine skeletons, 62 of them version 4.1.24 (three 4.1.17 for the max-win notice, one 4.1.23, and two 3.8 for the shared Power Play art), plus 8 frame sequences of 19 to 30 frames (fire-line win boxes, win blast, dynamite, coin spin, coin burst, burning plate). The rigs are small (most under 35 bones; the unlock pop-up has 66) and move whole pictures: symbols land in 0.3 s and play a 1.0 s win, the collector grows in 1.1 s, the chests have 45 short state animations each, the background runs one 233 s loop of light. No character is rigged limb by limb: the one full figure is a still swung on a rope. None of the skeletons is drawn in this run, because the project's renderer does not draw Spine 4.x; the real game screens show the motion's key states.
VariantsVariation is by recolour and by swap. One bonus chest in four colours; one collector in four colours and two heights; three chests from one drawing; four jackpot plates from one frame; five big-win tiers that differ only in the word; eight unlock screens from one scroll. Every reel symbol up to the portraits has a blurred twin for the spinning reel. A landscape and a portrait skeleton exist for the intro, chests, pots and pop-ups, over the same pictures.
Construction726 loose pictures in named folders, no atlas pages at all, at one scale (folder 100). Each feature is a folder with its skeletons and an images folder, and the client loads a feature's folder when it first needs it: 77 pictures and 5 skeletons arrived only during play. Backgrounds are single 3200x3200 squares cropped by the viewport. Text that carries language is baked into pictures marked _ml. Several pictures are shipped twice under different folders (the trail icons, the rope figure, the explosion).
ConsistencyStrong in colour and material: almost nothing leaves the orange-gold-brown family except by rule. Weaker in drawing hands: the realistic portraits, the cartoon props and a flat vector max-win notice are three styles, and there are three different coin designs. Leftover names from other Blueprint games (banana_trail, kong, genie_hammer_hit) and a ruby coin that reads SUPER for every pot show a shared production kit under the licensed skin (inference).

What to take from it Read

  • Read this as Blueprint Gaming's build BP_TheGooniesQuestForTreasure295. The market report ranks White Hat Studios' US build (WHS_TheGooniesQuestForTreasure2US94); the two share a title, and that they share their art is inference. It is not the Jackpot Royale version.
  • The licence carries the faces, the logo and two catchphrases; everything else is ordinary pirate-treasure art that a studio could make for its own theme: a cave, chests, coins, a map, a skeleton host. The lesson is how little likeness art (four portraits and one still figure) is needed to make a licensed game feel like the film.
  • One cool surface in a warm game: the navy reel board (#152035) is the only large cool area, so gold and orange symbols read without outlines. Worth copying as a layout rule.
  • Colour as code: three chest colours, four collector colours and four pot colours are each used the same way everywhere they appear (symbol, title, glow, pop-up), and cyan and acid green are reserved for anticipation and for the mystery and lock states.
  • Persistent progress drawn as objects, not meters: a parchment map of 20 steps above the reels and three physical chests beside them, each step paying off with its own titled unlock screen. For AI art work this is a set of small, flat, high-contrast icons plus one reusable scroll.
  • Variants by recolour and swap: one drawing per idea (chest, collector, plate, banner), then colour sets and word pictures. An art package planned this way needs few masters and many cheap derivatives, which suits generating a master and deriving variants.
  • Motion is cheap here: small Spine 4.1 rigs that move whole pictures, additive glow layers and a handful of short frame sequences; no rigged character. A studio can match this level of animation without character rigging.
  • Production notes for our own packages: lazy loading by feature folder keeps the first load light (649 pictures at start, 77 more in play); square 3200 px backgrounds serve both orientations; baked-in language pictures (_ml) make every language a new set of files.
  • Not seen in this run, so not to be relied on from it: free spins (Treasure Spins and One-Eyed Willy Spins), the Treasure Wheel, a big win and Power Play in play. Their art is in the package and read from the sheets only.

Art direction Read

StyleChunky 3D-look casino illustration with storybook proportions: rounded props (mug, pipe, barrel, boot, mushroom, pots), a big-headed family-animation character, and fairground lettering. The backdrop is a flat pattern, not a landscape. Nothing is straight: the frame, the board's outline and the banners all wobble or curl.
RenderingSmooth airbrushed volumes with hard outer edges for every object (soft edge 0.05 to 0.2: character 0.059, pipe 0.051, jackpot banners 0.114, high symbols 0.197), a green rim light under most props, and soft light for everything magical (rainbow effects 0.941, sparkles 0.825, bursts 0.827). Lettering has a two-tone face with a hard horizon, a thick rim and an extruded side.
ColourDark green and dark purple fields under gold and a full rainbow. Measured over the art files: near-black green #0b290b 17%, near-white #fcfbf7 11% (white effect sprites the game tints), dark magenta #36082e 10%, gold-orange #f2bb19 7%, wood brown #682b16 6%, purple #550867 3%, green #0c750e 2%. Gold marks what pays (coins, pots, WILD, frame, jackpot names); the rainbow marks what is magic (ribbon, progress meter, Collector panel, Jackpot Coin, transitions); and a five-step rainbow scale ranks things: purple, blue, green, red and gold for the royals and for the jackpot banners.
LightingObjects are lit from the top or top-right with a green bounce from below, as if standing in the clover field. The backdrop is darkest in the middle so the board glows against it. In the feature scene the light source is the rainbow ribbon itself.
AmbienceCosy, lucky and good-humoured: a pub sign in a clover patch at night. The feature scene is the same place enchanted, not a different world.
ShapesThe heart-shaped clover leaf is the module: backdrop leaves, the coin's stamp, the Scatter, the pipe's badge, the hat, the particles. Round bellies (pots, mug, barrel, coins, the character) against a thin wavy frame line; the curled scroll for jackpots; the arc for rainbows. The only sharp shape is the Booster arrow.
MaterialsPolished gold, cast iron, varnished wood, leather, felt, enamel and coloured glass, foam and beer, waxy leaves, light.
TypographyFour voices. The logo and jackpot names: gold serif capitals with a brown side. WILD, SCATTER, BOOST, FREE SPINS and the other headlines: a curly western poster face in yellow and orange with a red rim; captions in the same face in white with a wine outline, written as rhymes. Win tiers: tall flared capitals, dark with a neon outline. Numbers: the provider's bitmap fonts, Ultra in cream and gold (jackpot values, win amounts) and in purple and gold, and Ravie in yellow with a rainbow side (the Spin Progress counter). The low symbols 10 to A are fat slab serifs in single colours. Small interface text is the shell's Poppins (Regular, SemiBold, Bold).
MotionAll motion is Spine 4.2.43: 64 skeletons in one bundle file, plus 15 hand-drawn frame sequences (290 frames): five of white sparkle and smoke (112 frames), two of rainbow (45), two of white bursts (33), two of the pots (34), three coin and coin-shine sequences (45) and the GRAND highlight (21). The leprechaun is a 55-bone rig with separate eyes, brows, moustache, coat halves and limbs; the mug's effect has 51 bones; the big-win banner 92. Seen in play: the leprechaun standing large in front of the board as the game opens; a full mug over a reel and beer running down whole reels as stacked WILDs with foam on top; coins dropping from Golden Coins towards the pots; a thin line across a winning row with the amount in cream and gold numerals; FEATURE UNLOCKED over a small copy of the board when the Spin Progress counter reaches zero; the 10 FREE SPINS splash over a white burst; a rainbow wash across the whole screen into the purple scene; a large mug with WILD over the board before Wild Reels; +5 FREE SPINS on a retrigger; BIG WIN on its wooden plaque over a violet haze with Golden Coins tumbling across the screen. No skeleton frame is shown in this report, because the project's renderer is written for Spine 3.7.
VariantsTwo states of the whole stage from two backdrops and one tinted board (skins normal and special; holdAndWin for the board): green for the base game, purple with coloured clovers and a rainbow ribbon for Free Spins (seen) and, by the skin names, the Hold & Win. Frame in two states (gold; white with rainbow glow). Pots in two states with a 14-frame change. One character at two crops (1x2 symbol and full reel). Five jackpot banners as two mirrored shapes in four colours plus the Grand. Splashes in a normal and an upgraded skin.
ConstructionTwo 4096 px atlas pages hold 442 sprites, 290 of them animation frames, with 18 localised lettering files (en-GB), six loose textures and one skeleton bundle. The two backdrops are 1375x1255 pictures; the reel board ships in grey and is tinted. Symbols are layered where they move (mug in ten parts, Booster in four, coins with turn and shine frames) and single pictures where they do not (royals, the four props). Paytable pictures, the flattened logo, the numeral fonts and the interface come from the provider's shared services.
ConsistencyHigh. One clover module, one gold, one rainbow and one wobbling line run through backdrop, frame, symbols, interface and effects, and the green rim light ties the painted props to the green field. Seams: the win-tier lettering (dark with a neon outline) and the flat cartoon smoke are drawn in other hands than the gold-and-enamel world around them, and the white bursts are generic.

What to take from it Read

  • One character, used twice. The leprechaun is a single 55-bone rig of 20 small parts that serves as the intro figure, the 1x2 Collector and the full-reel Collector; there is no separate mascot beside the reels. For our packages: design the character as a symbol first and reuse the rig.
  • A theme can stand on a pattern instead of a painted scene. The backdrop is a dark lattice of shamrocks with a dozen loose leaves on bones; the second scene is the same layout in purple with a rainbow ribbon. Two 1375 px pictures and 11 leaf sprites make both stages, which is well within what image generation and a rig can deliver.
  • Ship neutral, tint in the game: the reel board is a grey wood picture coloured per state, and every sparkle and burst is white. One picture then serves the base game, Free Spins and the Hold & Win.
  • Let one cheap motif carry the brand: the heart-leaf clover is on the coin, the pipe, the hat, the Scatter, the backdrop and the confetti. A module like this keeps generated pieces looking like one game.
  • Use colour as a scale as well as a theme: the same five rainbow steps rank the royals and the jackpots, gold means payment and the rainbow means magic.
  • The persistent unlock meter costs little art: five flat pictograms, a watch, a ribbon and six caption files give the game its long-term structure (five features unlocked over 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 spins, the game's rules).
  • Anticipation art without mechanics: the pots fill with gold and grow rainbows in 14 and 20 drawn frames although, as the rules say, this has no influence on the trigger. It is a place where animation budget buys excitement directly.
  • Spend drawn frames on reusable white effects: 145 of the 290 frames are white sparkle, smoke and bursts that rigs tint and place on symbols, pots, jackpots and the backdrop.
  • From the same provider and framework as Fire Rail Express, 777 Hot Reels, Mega Cash Boost and Super Cash Boost (same shell, Poppins, Double Chance card, one skeleton bundle in Spine 4.2.43, packed 4096 px pages): of the five, this is the one with a character and a painted prop set, which shows the framework carries an illustrated theme as easily as a neon one.

A classic fruit machine set inside a volcano: glossy fruit, bells and sevens on calm teal cells, with all the heat, glow and budget given to four colours of burning fireball, three small colour-coded volcanoes and a great deal of simulated fire.

Art direction Read

StyleTwo registers side by side. The symbols are a traditional fruit set (two sevens, bell, melon, grapes, plum, orange, lemon, cherries) drawn as rounded, glossy 3D-look objects with a small engraved swirl each. The world around them is flat, hard-edged poster painting: a ruined temple for the base game, a crater under a spiral sky for the bonus. The feature pieces (fireballs, lava, eruptions) look simulated rather than drawn.
RenderingSymbols: smooth airbrushed volume, a hard white specular spot, a four-point sparkle, a thin gold rim on the premium ones, no outlines. Backgrounds: a few flat tones per shape, crisp edges, strong vignette to black. Effects: soft glowing frames on black grounds. Interface plates are clean teal enamel with a gold rim.
ColourWarm and dark overall. Measured over the game's own art: black #180908 24%, dark red #581413 14%, red #88172c 8%. Against that the reel cells are teal (#079a8f, #04655d), the one cool field in the base game, so warm symbols sit on their complement. Colour is also the rule system: red is the Multiplier volcano and fireball, green is Collect, blue is Double, orange is plain cash; the jackpots are orange (Grand), magenta (Major), blue (Minor) and green (Mini), and the multipliers are 2X blue, 3X green, 5X magenta. Fire leans to magenta and pink in the sky and haze (#780539, #d1065e) rather than staying orange.
LightingSymbols are lit from the top left with a soft shadow below. Everything that pays is self-lit: fireballs, lava, halos and frames glow past their own edges. Both backgrounds are lit from one hot source in the middle (the crack in the temple wall, the lava lake) and fall dark at the sides, which keeps the panels and the board readable.
AmbienceFamiliar and safe on the reels, loud and hot around them. The base game is an expectant temple chamber; the bonus drops into the crater, darker and redder, where gold numbers in fire rings are the only bright things. The opening is a short disaster film: eruption, flaming rocks at the camera, title, wipe to yellow.
ShapesRound and soft for everything collectable (fruit, bell, globes); square for everything structural (cells, frames, plates); the volcano cone is the one triangle and it is used as the game's badge. Frames are hairlines; the reel board has almost no body of its own.
MaterialsEnamel-like fruit, polished gold, lacquered sevens, plasma globes, lava and lava rock with glowing cracks, carved stone, cloud and smoke, teal enamel with gold rims.
TypographyThe logo and the labels MULTIPLIER, COLLECT, DOUBLE and the jackpot names are one flared serif display face with bevel and gold rim, coloured by meaning. Win amounts use a bitmap font of marbled gold serif numerals; fireball values use a second bitmap font, very condensed black figures with a yellow and orange outline. Five font files are embedded for running text (QTFrizQuad Bold, Noto Sans Condensed Bold, an Oswald cut with currency glyphs, and the provider's Lato and Gilroy).
MotionThirteen Spine 4.0 skeletons (binary) drive the scene, but most of what moves is frame sequences inside them: 30-frame loops for each fireball and each flame border, 30-frame fire frames for wins and anticipation, 22 to 38 frame bursts for hits, landings and eruptions, and 20 burning frames per letter of the win words. Seen in play: reels spin as vertical smears; a win dims the board, puts fire frames on the winning cells and counts a gold number up; a fireball flies from its cell to the volcano of its colour and the lava on that cone rises; at the trigger all three volcanoes erupt, rocks fly at the camera and the screen burns to the bonus, where two 5x3 reel sets respin and lock orange fireballs with values.
VariantsOne cone, three colours; one fireball, four colours, each with a matching flame border; one flared serif, six colour codes. Every reel symbol ships as a still, a spin-blur copy and as layers (body, gold contour, shadow). Backgrounds and menus have landscape and portrait versions. The bonus buy offers two cards: a mystery card and a hotter super card.
ConstructionThe 7 skeletons in the counts above are JSON files of a promotional overlay the demo host loads beside the game (listed under the provider interface, not read); the game's own 13 skeletons are binary files the tools do not count or draw. 76 textures and 1,913 named sprites were captured, 63 units of this game's art among them. Effects take most of the texture space: of 51 Spine atlas pages, 34 are opaque pages of frames on black (named _jpg, to be added as light) and several large effects ship as a colour page plus a black-and-white matte page instead of one page with alpha. The same small sequences are packed more than once (the hit burst three times, the embers twice), one copy per skeleton. Pages are WebP at quality 80 (as their names say), up to 2048 px. Symbol stills are about 150x130 px in a 180x158 cell.
ConsistencyStrong where it matters: the colour code is never broken, teal with gold is every number plate, the flared serif is every label. Three hands show otherwise: glossy rounded symbols, flat poster backgrounds and one soft painterly vortex behind the panels, and they are kept apart by where they appear, so they do not clash.

What to take from it Read

  • A leading game can be a plain fruit set: nine fruit-machine symbols and a wild. The art effort goes into the money objects (four fireballs) and the feature's targets (three volcanoes), not into the paytable.
  • Colour as rules: red, green and blue each mean one feature everywhere (fireball, border, volcano, label, buy card), and the jackpots and multipliers have fixed colours too. A player reads the state of the game from colour alone at thumbnail size.
  • Put warm symbols on a cool cell. The teal reel ground is the only large cool area and it makes every fruit and fireball stand off the board; the board itself is a hairline frame.
  • A meter can be a character: the lava level on each cone is the feature's progress display, and a halo over the crater says it is live. No figure was drawn for this game.
  • Change the place, not only the tint, for the bonus: temple interior for the base game, the crater for the bonus, each lit from one hot spot in the middle with dark sides for the panels.
  • Effects are frame sequences on black added as light, in 20 to 38 frames at about 150 to 500 px. That is a production method an AI art pipeline can follow: generate short fire and burst loops on black, no alpha needed.
  • Two number styles that cannot be confused: marbled gold serif numerals for wins, condensed black figures with a fire outline for values on fireballs.
  • What to avoid copying: the same sequences packed several times and mattes shipped as separate pages cost texture memory; our own packages should share one copy.

A two-sided cartoon mythology: Zeus's blue storm sky against Hades's red lava underworld, drawn as stylised 3D-look paintings with polished gold as the trim that holds both sides together, and a third, candy-bright register reserved for the POP prize feature.

Art direction Read

StyleStylised 3D-look digital painting in a family-animation manner. Characters have large heads, barrel torsos and big hands; Zeus is round and friendly, Hades angular with spikes, pointed ears and claws; Pegasus is cute and pastel. Low symbols are extruded slab-serif letters. Architecture (temple, prize bar, logo slab) is chunky carved stone with Greek key borders.
RenderingSmooth gradients that read like a soft 3D render, clean hard silhouettes and no line outlines anywhere. Detail is concentrated in faces, gold trim and jewellery; backgrounds are soft-focus paintings kept low in detail so the board reads first. Effects are the opposite: thin, sharp, bright shapes with glow.
ColourTwo opposed families and one shared metal. Zeus and the base game: cyan and blue (#22efff, #2b7cf2, #3986ce, #324382). Hades and free spins: red, orange and dark crimson (#8e1f15, #540e19, #d92d11, #f49419). Gold (#f9ea77, #f49419) trims every symbol and frame on both sides. Purple marks what belongs to neither god (the VS coin's galaxy, the Ace, cloth shadows). Lime, pink and cyan neon appear only on the three POP prize fields. Measured over the game's own art: vivid (saturation 63%), mid-tone, warm 54% against cool 40%.
LightingEach side is lit by its own element: cool cyan light from lightning on Zeus pieces, warm light from fire on Hades pieces, usually against the opposite temperature in the shadows (purple-blue shadows on warm skin). Bevels are top-lit. Lightning, fire, frame edges and eyes are emissive and drawn as separate additive layers, so glow is a layer, not paint.
AmbienceA playful rivalry rather than a solemn myth: loud, bright, friendly menace. The base game is an airy storm sky, calm between flashes; free spins is a hot, busy underworld of lava falls, chains and stone pillars. POP moments switch to soap bubbles and pastel rainbow, closer to a casual mobile game than to the Greek set.
ShapesRounded and chunky throughout, with angular accents (spikes, zigzag lightning, flames) reserved for power and danger. Frames are thin rails with Greek-key corners; figures break out of their frames.
MaterialsPolished gold with engraved Greek key, white cloth in broad folds, matte skin, sculpted hair in large locks, blue marble and ice-blue crystal, cut gems, lava and fire, cloud, bone and skulls, soap bubbles and glossy candy plastic for POP.
TypographyDisplay lettering is drawn art, not type: ice-blue faceted ZEUS, gold flaming HADES and a gold bubble POP in the logo; bevelled gold words for the win tiers; extruded letters with a gold rim for A, K, Q and J. Seventeen typefaces are embedded for running text and numbers, most of them the provider's interface faces.
MotionSpine 3.7 skeletons carry almost all movement: symbols have landing (0.5 s), win (1.5 s) and sometimes idle and anticipation animations; the two mascots have six each (idle, idle break, two annoyed, two win). Fire, lightning, hair and sparkle are short hand-drawn frame sequences (3 to 21 frames) played inside the rigs. The expanding VS symbol plays as a duel with two outcomes, fire for Hades and lightning for Zeus. The scene transition is a video-like run of 25 full frames that shows Hades, then Zeus, then breaks open from the centre.
VariantsNearly everything exists twice, as a blue base-game version and a red free-spins recolour: backgrounds, reel frame, backing, rails, bars, reel highlights and win-meter effects. Each reel symbol ships as a sharp still, a vertically smeared still (probably the spin blur: inference) and a skeleton. Win tiers are split between the gods: Zeus carries Mega and Sensational, Hades carries Nice and Superb. The three POP result banners (Burst magenta, Spark blue, Snap green) are one design recoloured.
Construction3,550 named sprites on 243 textures, 39 skeletons. A character is 73 to 221 parts, with a painted shadow piece for nearly every overlapping part and separate additive glow layers; meshes are used for cloth, hair and faces, regions for rigid parts. The four royals share one 9 to 10 part template: a coloured letter face with flickering lightning at rest, and a lava-cell picture that fills the face, clipped to the letter, during the win. Atlas textures are shipped at 50 to 69% of the source art and as 8-bit palette PNGs. The reel board is deliberately plain (flat backing, thin frame, gold dividers); the prize bar is its one decorated piece.
ConsistencyThe Greek set is tight: one rendering manner, one frame construction, one gold. Three things sit outside it and look like shared platform art or a different hand: the POP bubble symbol and banners (glossy candy style), the flat gold title plates in the big-win atlas, and loose shared sprites such as number fonts, coins and a red envelope (inference).

What to take from it Read

  • Colour does the storytelling: one hue family per side, the opposite temperature in the shadows, and one metal shared by both. A recolour of the same asset is enough to say which mode you are in.
  • Glow, shadow and fire are separate layers on every character. That is what lets a painted figure animate in Spine without repainting, and it is the part a generated image does not give you by itself.
  • The board is kept quiet so that symbols and characters carry the detail; decoration is spent on one piece (the prize bar).
  • A feature can have its own visual register (POP's candy pastel) as long as it is confined to that feature's symbols, bar fields and banners.
